question: Why has ISRO proposed the development of a third launch pad beyond the existing facilities at Sriharikota?

options.text: To serve exclusively as a data relay hub for enhancing satellite telemetry
To accommodate space tourism missions under future commercial programmes
To provide backup support in case of emergency ground failures during launches
To handle increasing launch frequency and capacity for missions involving SSLV, Gaganyaan, and commercial payloads

solution:
The correct answer is __**To handle increasing launch frequency and capacity for missions involving SSLV, Gaganyaan, and commercial payloads**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)** has proposed the development of a third launch pad to address the **increasing demand for satellite launches** and ensure operational efficiency.
 
• The existing launch pads at **Sriharikota** are primarily used for missions involving the PSLV (Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle) and GSLV (Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle) series.
 
• The third launch pad will cater to **Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV)** missions, which are designed for launching smaller satellites into orbit, as well as the upcoming **Gaganyaan** (India's human spaceflight mission).
 
• With the **expansion of commercial payload launches** under the "New Space India Limited (NSIL)" initiative, a new launch pad is critical to meeting global demand and generating revenue for ISRO.
 
• The third pad will also support **higher launch frequency**, ensuring a faster turnaround time between missions to accommodate both government and commercial clients.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV):**

 
 
• The SSLV is a smaller, cost-effective launcher developed by ISRO for deploying small satellites into low Earth orbit.
 
• It is designed to cater to the growing demand for small satellite launches, including nano and microsatellites.
 
• The SSLV is considered a key asset for commercial clients seeking affordable and quick satellite deployment.
 
 
 
• **Gaganyaan Mission:**
 
 
• The Gaganyaan is India’s first human spaceflight mission, aiming to carry Indian astronauts (Vyomanauts) into space by 2024.

subject: GK
question: What is the primary function of the Solar Wind Ion Spectrometer (SWIS), included in the ASPEX payload on Aditya-L1?

options.text: Records UV imagery of solar flare activity
Monitors tremors and vibrations on the solar surface
Observes changes in the Earth's geomagnetic field
Detects directional flow of solar wind protons and helium nuclei

solution:
The correct answer is __**Detects directional flow of solar wind protons and helium nuclei**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Solar Wind Ion Spectrometer (SWIS)**, a part of the ASPEX (Aditya Solar wind Particle Experiment) payload on the **Aditya-L1 mission**, is designed to measure the **directional flow and energy distribution** of solar wind ions.
 
• The solar wind primarily consists of **protons, helium nuclei (alpha particles),** and other charged particles emitted from the Sun's corona. SWIS helps analyze their properties.
 
• SWIS is crucial for understanding the **spatial and temporal variations** in the solar wind, which directly affects space weather and geomagnetic activities on Earth.
 
• The instrument provides data on the **velocity, density, and composition** of solar wind ions, offering insights into the Sun's influence on interplanetary space.
 
• This data is critical for studying **solar-terrestrial interactions**, including the effects on satellite communications, navigation systems, and power grids.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Aditya-L1 Mission:**

 
 
• India's first dedicated solar mission, launched by **ISRO (Indian Space Research Organisation)**, aims to study the Sun from the **Lagrange Point 1 (L1)**, approximately 1.5 million kilometers from Earth.
 
• The spacecraft is equipped with seven payloads, including instruments to study the Sun's **photosphere, chromosphere, corona**, and solar wind.
 
• The mission aims to provide critical data for understanding **space weather phenomena** and their impact on Earth's environment.
 
 
 
• **ASPEX Payload:**
 
 
• ASPEX (Aditya Solar wind Particle Experiment) comprises instruments like SWIS that focus on studying the **solar wind and energetic particles** emitted by the Sun.
 
• This payload helps in understanding the variations in the solar wind and how these changes influence the Earth's magnetosphere.
 
 
 
• **Solar Wind:**
 
 
• The solar wind is a continuous stream of charged particles, primarily **protons and electrons**, flowing outward from the Sun's corona.
 
• The solar wind interacts with the Earth's magnetosphere, causing phenomena like **geomagnetic storms and auroras**.
 
 
 
• **Lagrange Point L1:**
 
 
• The **L1 point** is a stable location in space where the gravitational forces of the Sun and Earth balance the centrifugal force experienced by a spacecraft.
 
• Placing Aditya-L1 at this point ensures a **continuous and unobstructed view of the Sun**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option 1:** "Records UV imagery of solar flare activity" is incorrect as this function is performed by other instruments like the **Solar Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (SUIT)**.
 
• **Option 2:** "Monitors tremors and vibrations on the solar surface" is incorrect as this is related to helioseismology, studied by instruments like the **Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI)**.
 
• **Option 3:** "Observes changes in the Earth's geomagnetic field" is incorrect since this is monitored by ground-based observatories and space missions dedicated to Earth's magnetosphere.
 
• **Option 4:** "Detects directional flow of solar wind protons and helium nuclei" is correct as it directly relates to the function of the **Solar Wind Ion Spectrometer (SWIS)**.

question: The NISAR satellite mission is primarily related to which type of imaging?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Radar imaging**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **NISAR** is an acronym for **NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar**, representing a high-profile joint collaboration between the **United States (NASA)** and **India (ISRO)**.
 
• The mission is specifically designed to perform **radar imaging** using a **dual-frequency** system consisting of **L-band** and **S-band** Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) instruments.
 
• The primary scientific objective is to observe and measure **Earth’s dynamic surfaces**, including changes in **ice sheets**, **forest biomass**, and **land deformation** caused by earthquakes or volcanoes.
 
• Unlike optical sensors, **SAR** technology allows the satellite to capture data with high precision regardless of **weather conditions**, cloud cover, or the absence of sunlight (day or night).
 
• The satellite is scheduled to be launched into a **Sun-synchronous orbit** and will map the entire global land and ice masses every **12 days** to provide consistent time-series data.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR)**:

 
 
• This is an **active sensing** technique where the satellite transmits its own microwave signals and records the reflection to create **two-dimensional** or **three-dimensional** images of the surface.
 
• The **L-band** (provided by NASA) has a wavelength of approximately **24 cm**, which is ideal for penetrating dense foliage and measuring ground movement.
 
• The **S-band** (provided by ISRO) has a wavelength of about **12 cm** and is useful for monitoring light vegetation and heavy weather conditions.
 
 
 
• **Optical Imaging**:
 
 
• Requires **visible light** to function; hence, it is ineffective during the night and cannot see through **clouds** or **thick smoke**.
 
 
 
• **Spectroscopy**:
 
 
• Involves analyzing the **chemical composition** and physical properties of matter by studying its interaction with the electromagnetic spectrum, often used in **hyperspectral imaging** missions like **HysIS**.
 
 
 
• **Sample Return**:
 
 
• Refers to missions that physically collect material from extra-terrestrial bodies and return it to Earth, such as the **OSIRIS-REx** or **Hayabusa** missions.

question: What is the benefit of the NavIC system?

options.text: Offers regional navigation and positioning services

solution:
The correct answer is __**Offers regional navigation and positioning services**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation)** is an independent satellite navigation system developed by **India's Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)**.
 
• It provides **regional navigation and positioning services**, covering the Indian mainland and a region extending approximately 1,500 km beyond its borders.
 
• NavIC is designed to provide two levels of service: **Standard Positioning Service (SPS)** for all users and **Restricted Service (RS)** for authorized users, such as military operations.
 
• It is an alternative to systems like the US-based GPS (Global Positioning System), ensuring **self-reliance in navigation services**.
 
• The system offers high accuracy, with a position accuracy of better than **20 meters** in the coverage area, which is suitable for applications in disaster management, navigation for vehicles, and tracking services.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Development and Features of NavIC:**

 
 
• NavIC is also known as the **Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS)**.
 
• The system comprises **seven satellites** in geostationary and geosynchronous orbits, with ground stations monitoring and controlling the satellites.
 
• It was developed to reduce dependency on foreign navigation systems and ensure **secure navigation services** for India.
 
• The first satellite, IRNSS-1A, was launched in **July 2013**, and the system became operational in **2018**.
 
 
 
• **Applications of NavIC:**
 
 
• Used for **civilian navigation**, including road, sea, and air transport.
 
• Plays a critical role in **disaster management** by providing accurate location data for rescue operations.
 
• Supports applications in **agriculture, fisheries, and mining** by enabling precise positioning and timing services.
 
• Used in **scientific research**, including atmospheric studies and geodetic measurements.
 
• Offers benefits for **military operations** by providing encrypted services to authorized users.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Global Navigation Systems:**
 
 
• **Global Positioning System (GPS):** Developed by the United States, GPS offers global coverage and is widely used worldwide.
 
• **GLONASS:** Russia's navigation system, offering global coverage with a focus on high latitudes.
 
• **Galileo:** Europe's satellite navigation system providing high precision globally.
 
• **BeiDou:** China's navigation system offering global and regional coverage.
 
• **NavIC:** Focuses on regional coverage, offering comparable accuracy within its service area.
 
 
 
• **Future Enhancements:**
 
 
• ISRO plans to upgrade NavIC by adding **L1 band support** to make it compatible with international standards and devices.
 
• Efforts are being made to integrate NavIC into **smartphones** and other consumer devices to enhance adoption.
 
• Expansion of its applications in **commercial sectors**, including logistics and transportation, is underway.

question: What is the major benefit of the Indian Data Relay Satellite System (IDRSS)?

options.text: Real-time communication with low Earth orbit satellites and astronauts

solution:
The correct answer is __**Real-time communication with low Earth orbit satellites and astronauts**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Indian Data Relay Satellite System (IDRSS)** is a planned constellation of communication satellites developed by the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)** to track and maintain constant contact with Indian satellites.
 
• It is primarily designed to facilitate **real-time, continuous data transfer** between ground stations and satellites operating in **Low Earth Orbit (LEO)**, which otherwise have very short windows of visibility to terrestrial antennas.
 
• The system is fundamental to the success of the **Gaganyaan mission**, as it allows for uninterrupted **voice and data communication** with **astronauts** and the **crew module** throughout their orbit around the Earth.
 
• By positioning **IDRSS** satellites in the **Geostationary Orbit (GEO)** at an altitude of nearly **36,000 kilometers**, they can act as a bridge, relaying critical **telemetry**, **tracking**, and **command (TT&C)** data without the coverage gaps inherent in ground-based networks.
 
• The deployment of this network ensures that **mission controllers** at the **Satish Dhawan Space Centre** can monitor the health of the spacecraft and receive scientific data in high-definition without delay.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Deep Space Exploration**

 
 
• Unlike **LEO** relay systems, missions to the **Moon** or **Mars** like **Chandrayaan** and **Mangalyaan** rely on the **Indian Deep Space Network (IDSN)**, which uses massive **32-meter** parabolic antennas for long-distance communication.
 
 
 
• **Solar Energy from Space**
 
 
• This refers to **Space-Based Solar Power (SBSP)**, a conceptual technology that harvests **renewable energy** in orbit to transmit it back to Earth via **microwaves**, which is not the function of **IDRSS**.
 
 
 
• **Satellite Internet Access**
 
 
• Providing **broadband** to **rural areas** is the objective of **High Throughput Satellites (HTS)** such as **GSAT-11** and **GSAT-20**, which utilize multiple **spot beams** to deliver high-speed data directly to consumers.

__
 
• The **Second Stage (GS2)** of the **GSLV-F16** launch vehicle was officially flagged off in **March 2025**, specifically on **March 4, 2025**.
 
• The flagging-off ceremony took place at the **ISRO Propulsion Complex (IPRC)** located in **Mahendragiri**, Tamil Nadu, marking a critical step in the assembly of the rocket.
 
• The **GSLV-F16** mission is dedicated to launching the **NISAR** (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) satellite, a major international collaboration between the **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)** and the **National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)**.
 
• The **GS2 stage** is a liquid-propellant stage that utilizes the **Vikas Engine**, which is the workhorse of Indian liquid propulsion systems, burning a combination of **UDMH** (fuel) and **Nitrogen Tetroxide** (oxidizer).
 
• This stage is transported from **Mahendragiri** to the **Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC) SHAR** in **Sriharikota** for final integration with other stages of the launch vehicle.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **NISAR Mission Overview:**

 
 
• It is a **Dual-frequency (L-band and S-band)** Radar Imaging Satellite designed to map the entire globe in 12 days.
 
• The mission aims to provide spatially and temporally consistent data for understanding changes in **Earth ecosystems**, **ice mass**, **vegetation biomass**, and **natural hazards** like earthquakes and tsunamis.
 
 
 
• **GSLV (Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle):**
 
 
• The **GSLV Mark II** is a three-stage vehicle consisting of a solid first stage, a liquid second stage (GS2), and a **Cryogenic Upper Stage (CUS)**.
 
• The **GS2 stage** provides the necessary thrust after the burnout of the solid boosters to propel the payload into a **Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO)** or **Sun-Synchronous Orbit (SSO)**.
 
 
 
• **IPRC Mahendragiri:**
 
 
• It is the lead center for **Liquid Propulsion Systems** and is responsible for the assembly, integration, and testing of liquid engines and stages for ISRO launch vehicles.

question: Identify the pigment that gives blood its colour.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Haemoglobin**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Hemoglobin **is the pigment responsible for the **red colour of blood**.
 
• It's a **protein** found in **red blood cells**.
 
• **Hemoglobin** carries **oxygen** from the **lungs to body tissues** and returns **carbon dioxide** to the **lungs**.
 
• The **iron-containing heme group** within **haemoglobin** gives blood its r**ed colour**. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ferritin**

 
 
• **Ferritin** is a **protein** that **stores iron in cells**.
 
• It helps **regulate iron levels **in **the body**.
 
• Composed of **24 subunits** forming a **spherical structure**.
 
• Measurement of **ferritin levels in blood indicates iron status**.
 
• **Low levels** may indicate** iron deficiency**; **high levels**,** iron overload **or other conditions.
 
 
 
• **Chlorophyll**
 
 
• **Green pigment** found in **chloroplasts** of **plants and algae**.
 
• Essential for **photosynthesis**, converting **sunlight into chemical energ**y.
 
• Absorbs light in **blue and red wavelengths**, **reflecting green light**.
 
• Captures light energy to synthesize **carbohydrates** from **CO2 and water**.
 
• **Molecular structure** includes a **porphyrin ring** with a **magnesium ion**, giving it its **green colour**.
 
 
 
• **Xanthophyll**
 
 
• **Yellow pigment **found in **plants and algae**.
 
• Contributes to **leaf colouration**, **especially in autumn**.
 
• Doesn't directly participate in **photosynthesis**.
 
• Helps dissipate excess **light energy, protecting chlorophyll**.
 
• Also provides **photoprotection against UV radiation.**

subject: GK
question: During which phase of the cell cycle does metabolic changes assemble the cytoplasmic material required for mitosis and cytokinesis?
solution:
The Correct Answer is** __G2 Phase__.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The G2 phase of the cell cycle **involves metabolic changes that assemble **cytoplasmic materials **necessary for** mitosis and cytokinesis**.
 
• This phase is followed by the **M phase**, where **nuclear division (mitosis) **is followed by **cell division (cytokinesis)**.
 
• Eukaryotic cells undergo a series of stages collectively known as the cell cycle, which includes** two gap phases (G1 and G2)**, an **S phase (synthesis)** where genetic material is duplicated, and an M phase where mitosis partitions the genetic material and the cell divides.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

__
 
• During **mitosis, chromosomes **replicated during the **S phase **are divided to ensure that each daughter cell receives a copy of **every chromosome**.
 
• This process results in the production of **two daughter cells **with the same genetic component as the parent cell.
 
• In actively dividing animal cells, the entire process typically takes about one hour.
 
• The final cellular division results in the formation of two new cells.
 
• Following mitosis is Meiosis II, where Meiosis I is a reduction division resulting in haploid cells with one copy of each chromosome.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **G1 phase:** During this phase, metabolic changes prepare the cell for division. At a specific point called the restriction point, the cell commits to division and enters the S phase.
 
• **S phase:** In this phase, DNA synthesis occurs, resulting in the replication of the genetic material. Each chromosome now consists of two sister chromatids.
 
• **G2 phase: **Metabolic changes in this phase assemble the cytoplasmic materials necessary for mitosis and cytokinesis.
 
• **M phase:** This phase involves nuclear division (mitosis) followed by cell division (cytokinesis).

subject: GK
question: Which enzyme primarily is responsible for joining "Okazaki fragments" during the DNA replication process?
solution:
The correct answer is __**DNA ligase**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **DNA ligase** is an essential enzyme involved in DNA replication and repair processes, particularly responsible for joining Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand.
 
• Okazaki fragments are short DNA sequences synthesized on the lagging strand during replication. DNA ligase seals the gaps between these fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds.
 
• DNA ligase plays a critical role in maintaining the integrity of the DNA molecule by ensuring that the newly synthesized DNA strands are continuous and stable.
 
• This enzyme works by catalyzing the formation of a covalent bond between the 3’-hydroxyl group of one nucleotide and the 5’-phosphate group of another nucleotide.
 
• In addition to DNA replication, DNA ligase is also involved in processes such as DNA repair mechanisms, including base excision repair and double-strand break repair.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **DNA polymerase:**

 
 
• DNA polymerase is the enzyme responsible for synthesizing new strands of DNA by adding nucleotides to the 3’ end of a growing DNA strand during replication.
 
• It primarily works in a 5’ to 3’ direction and requires a primer to initiate DNA synthesis.
 
• While it synthesizes Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand, it does not join them; this task is performed by DNA ligase.
 
 
 
• **Helicase:**
 
 
• Helicase is an enzyme that unwinds the double-stranded DNA molecule at the replication fork, creating two single strands that can serve as templates for replication.
 
• It breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, separating the two strands and allowing the replication machinery to access the DNA.
 
• Helicase does not directly participate in the joining of Okazaki fragments.
 
 
 
• **Primase:**
 
 
• Primase is an RNA polymerase enzyme that synthesizes short RNA primers on the lagging strand during DNA replication.
 
• These primers provide a starting point for DNA polymerase to begin synthesizing DNA.
 
• Primase is not involved in the joining of Okazaki fragments; its role is limited to primer synthesis.
 
 
 
• **Okazaki fragments:**
 
 
• Okazaki fragments are short DNA sequences synthesized discontinuously on the lagging strand during replication.
 
• These fragments are later joined together by DNA ligase to form a continuous strand.
 
• The lagging strand is synthesized discontinuously because DNA synthesis can only occur in the 5’ to 3’ direction, requiring frequent initiation by RNA primers.

subject: GK
question: Which cell organelle is an overlapping membranous sac with ER-like thickness that helps in processing and packaging protein and lipid molecules, especially stable proteins?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Golgi apparatus.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**__**Golgi Apparatus:**__

__
 
• The Golgi apparatus has multiple names such as the **Golgi complex or Golgi body.**
 
• The name is given on the name of the scientist, who discovered the organelle, i.e. Camillo Golgi.
 
• It is **found in all the eukaryotic cells**, plants as well as animals.
 
• They are membrane-bound organelles present in the cytosol of the cell.
 
• The Golgi body comprises 5 to 8 cup-shaped, series of compartments known as **cisternae**. Cisternae is a flattened, disk-shaped, stacked pouches that make up the Golgi apparatus. A Golgi stack mostly contains 4 to 8 cisternae. However, ~60 cisternae are found in some protists. A mammalian cell contains ~40 to 100 stacks of cisternae.
 
• Animal cells generally contain around 10 to 20 Golgi stacks per cell, which are connected by tubular connections.
 
• Golgi complex is mostly found near the nucleus.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/8a66665c8b7d6a84497438e44c0511f463d9d862ee49c9ea1be606ed25af9562.png] 

**Functions of Golgi Bodies:**__

 
• Its main function is the **packaging and secretion of proteins.** 
 
• It receives proteins from Endoplasmic Reticulum. It packages it into **membrane-bound vesicles**, which are then transported to various destinations, such as lysosomes, plasma membrane or secretion.
 
• They also take part in the** transport of lipids **and the formation of lysosomes.
 
• **Post-translational modification and enzymatic processing** occur near the membrane surface in Golgi bodies, e.g. phosphorylation, glycosylation, etc.

**Golgi Bodies Functions:**

__
 
• **Its main function is the packaging and secretion of proteins**.

**Golgi Apparatus:**

 
• The Golgi apparatus has multiple names such as the **Golgi complex or Golgi body.**
 
• The name is given on the **name of the scientist, who discovered the organelle, i.e. Camillo Golgi.**
 
• It is found in **all the eukaryotic cells, plants as well as animals.**
 
• They are membrane-bound organelles present in the cytosol of the cell.
 
• The Golgi body comprises 5 to 8 cup-shaped, series of compartments known as cisternae. Cisternae is a flattened, disk-shaped, stacked pouches that make up the Golgi apparatus. A Golgi stack mostly contains 4 to 8 cisternae. However, ~60 cisternae are found in some protists. A mammalian cell contains ~40 to 100 stacks of cisternae.

question: Which thin flexible barrier separates the internal environment of the cell from the extracellular fluid?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Plasma membrane.**__

__
 
• The plasma membrane is selectively permeable because hydrophobic molecules and small polar molecules can diffuse through the lipid layer, but ions and large polar molecules cannot. 
 
• Integral membrane proteins enable ions and large polar molecules to pass through the membrane by passive or active transport.
 
• Selectively permeable means a membrane allows the passage of some molecules or ions and inhibits the passage of others.
 
• The capacity to filter molecular transport in this manner is called selective permeability. This is also called differential permeability.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/0c96da9b13f2ad86d8f363702005a8221c34d877ec17bae0442afd43fdc5e6ea.png]

• Other types of membranes on the basis of permeability:

 
 
• Impermeable membrane: Substances of any type can not pass through them.
 
• Permeable membranes: Substances of any type can pass through them.
 
• Semi-permeable membrane: These are the membrane which permits the movement of only solvent molecules through them.

• Lysosomes work as the waste-discarding structures of the cell by processing undesirable materials and degrading them, both from the exterior of the cell and waste constituents inside the cell.
 
• But sometimes, the digestive enzymes may end up damaging the lysosomes themselves, and this can cause the cell to die.

• **Polysome:** Many **ribosomes may associate with a single mRNA** to form **multiple copies of a polypeptide simultaneously**.

subject: GK
question: What is the percentage of proteins in the cell membrane?
solution:
The correct answer is __**40-60%**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **A typical plasma membrane** comprises roughly equal proportions of proteins and lipids, with each component accounting for approximately 50% of the membrane's composition. However, these percentages can vary depending on the cell type and its specific functions.
 
• For instance, membranes involved in ATP production, such as those found within mitochondria and chloroplasts, are enriched in proteins, constituting approximately 75% of their composition.
 
• Proteins play crucial roles in executing specific functions within the membrane.
 
• There are two primary classes of membrane-associated proteins: peripheral and integral membrane proteins. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The cell membrane** consists of phospholipids, which are amphipathic molecules. These molecules feature two hydrophobic fatty acid chains attached to a hydrophilic head group containing phosphate.
 
• Because the fatty acid tails repel water, phospholipids naturally arrange themselves into bilayers when in an aqueous environment.
 
• Being semipermeable, the cell membrane allows certain molecules to pass through its lipid bilayer while blocking others. It plays a critical role in regulating the transport of substances into and out of the cell.
 
• The membrane selectively hinders the diffusion of highly charged particles like ions, as well as large molecules such as sugars and amino acids.

question: What do you call the fluid matrix filling in the cell?
solution:
The correct answer is **__Cytoplasm.__**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Cytoplasm** is a** gelatinous fluid **occupying the **space within a cell,** which serves as the region between the **plasma membrane and the nucleus**.
 
• It encompasses both the** cytosol,** a semi-fluid portion, and various organelles suspended within it.
 
• Notably,** prokaryotic cells **lack membrane-bound organelles characteristic of eukaryotic cells, such as mitochondria or endoplasmic reticulum.
 
• Instead, their cytoplasm contains various structures essential for cellular functions, albeit without the distinct membrane boundaries seen in eukaryotic organelles.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ribosomes** are large ribonucleoprotein complexes found ubiquitously in all cells. Comprising both RNA and proteins, ribosomes play a crucial role in translating genetic information stored in mRNA into polypeptide chains.
 
• **Plasmids** are small, extrachromosomal DNA molecules present within a cell, physically distinct from the chromosomal DNA and capable of replicating independently. They often carry non-essential genes that may confer advantages such as antibiotic resistance.
 
• Discovered in 1897 by Italian physician Camillo Golgi, the Golgi complex is a cellular organelle consisting of five to eight flattened membrane-bound sacs known as cisternae. It plays a vital role in processing, modifying, and packaging proteins and lipids for transport within the cell or secretion outside the cell.

question: The main function of centriole is:

options.text: to help plant cell for multiplication
to help cell division in animal cell
to maintain rigidity in plant cell
to maintain mineral composition in bacterial cell

solution:
The correct answer is __**to help cell division in animal cell**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Centrioles** are paired** barrel-shaped organelles f**ound in the **cytoplasm of animal cells**, typically situated near the **nuclear envelope**.
 
• They play a crucial role in organizing **microtubules**, which act as the cell's structural framework.
 
• Additionally, centrioles aid in determining the positioning of the nucleus and other organelles within the cell.
 
• Each centriole resides within the centrosome, an area of the cytoplasm located adjacent to the nucleus.
 
• The centrosome, considered an organelle, contains two centrioles.
 
• Composed of microtubules, centrioles are integral to cell division processes and are essential for maintaining cellular structure and function.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Centrioles **consist of **nine groups of microtubule triplets** arranged in a cylindrical configuration, a detailed structure that can only be observed under an electron microscope.
 
• These microtubule triplets are interconnected and oriented at right angles to each other, contributing to the centriole's overall stability and function.
 
• However, there are exceptions to this typical centriolar organization. For instance, in the embryos of Drosophila melanogaster, nine pairs of microtubules are formed instead of the usual microtubule triplets.
 
• Similarly, premature embryos and sperm cells of Caenorhabditis elegans exhibit a unique arrangement of nine single microtubules, deviating from the standard centriolar structure observed in most animal cells.

question: Who explained the structure of protein?
solution:
The Correct Answer is **__Pauling and Corey__.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Linus Pauling** is recognized for successfully predicting regular **protein secondary structures **based on** hydrogen bonding,** an idea originally proposed by **William Astbury**.
 
• **Pauling and Corey** formulated a model for the conformation of **fibrous proteins called beta-keratins**, where the polypeptide adopts an extended zig-zag configuration rather than a coil, such as in the alpha-helix.
 
• All proteins in the human body can be synthesized from permutations of just **20 amino acids**.
 
• There are seven primary types of proteins: antibodies, contractile proteins, enzymes, hormonal proteins, structural proteins, storage proteins, and transport proteins.
 
• A protein molecule is composed of a lengthy chain of these amino acids, each linked to its adjacent amino acid through a covalent peptide bond.
 
• Hence, proteins are also referred to as polypeptides. Each type of protein possesses a distinctive sequence of amino acids, which remains identical from one molecule to another.
 
• Numerous proteins with diverse functions are known, each characterized by its specific amino acid sequence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Emil Fischer**, a German organic chemist, is credited with the** discovery of caffeine **and other related purines.
 
• Additionally, he conducted extensive research on the molecular structures of sugars and proteins, earning him the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1902.
 
• **Proteins** are comprised of amino acids, with **21 naturally occurring variants**.
 
• Secondary protein structures are stabilized by hydrogen bonding. The characteristics of protein strands vary depending on the type of hydrogen bonding present, with two common types being the alpha helix and beta sheet.
 
• The alpha helix is a right-handed coiled secondary protein structure, where the substituents of the amino acids extend outward.
 
• Hydrogen bonds form between the carbonyl oxygen and the four NH bonds below it, contributing to the stability of the helix.

subject: GK
question:
Sequence the following stages of cellular respiration:

1. Electron Transport Chain

2. Glycolysis

3. Krebs Cycle

4. Pyruvate Oxidation
solution:
The correct answer is __**2 - 4 - 3 - 1**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Glycolysis (2):** This is the first stage of cellular respiration that occurs in the cytoplasm. It involves the breakdown of glucose into two molecules of pyruvate, generating a small amount of ATP and NADH.
 
• **Pyruvate Oxidation (4):** The pyruvate molecules produced during glycolysis are transported into the mitochondria, where they are converted into acetyl-CoA. This process also produces NADH and releases carbon dioxide.
 
• **Krebs Cycle (3):** The acetyl-CoA enters the Krebs cycle (or Citric Acid Cycle) in the mitochondrial matrix. This cycle generates high-energy molecules such as NADH and FADH2 while releasing carbon dioxide as a byproduct.
 
• **Electron Transport Chain (1):** This is the final stage of cellular respiration, which occurs in the inner mitochondrial membrane. NADH and FADH2 donate electrons to the chain, driving the production of a large amount of ATP through oxidative phosphorylation.
 
• The sequence of cellular respiration is **Glycolysis → Pyruvate Oxidation → Krebs Cycle → Electron Transport Chain**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Glycolysis:**

 
 
• Occurs in the cytoplasm and is an anaerobic process (does not require oxygen).
 
• Produces a net gain of 2 ATP molecules, 2 NADH molecules, and 2 pyruvate molecules per glucose molecule.
 
• This process is the universal pathway for energy generation in both aerobic and anaerobic organisms.
 
 
 
• **Pyruvate Oxidation:**
 
 
• Occurs in the mitochondria in the presence of oxygen.
 
• Each pyruvate molecule is converted into acetyl-CoA, producing 1 NADH molecule and releasing 1 molecule of carbon dioxide.
 
• The acetyl-CoA acts as a substrate for the Krebs Cycle.
 
 
 
• **Krebs Cycle:**
 
 
• Also known as the Citric Acid Cycle or TCA Cycle, it is a series of enzyme-catalyzed chemical reactions.
 
• Generates 2 ATP molecules, 6 NADH molecules, and 2 FADH2 molecules per glucose molecule.
 
• Releases carbon dioxide as a waste product.
 
 
 
• **Electron Transport Chain:**
 
 
• Located in the inner mitochondrial membrane, this stage requires oxygen as the final electron acceptor.
 
• Electrons from NADH and FADH2 pass through protein complexes, creating a proton gradient.
 
• ATP synthase utilizes this gradient to produce ATP, with water being formed as a byproduct.
 
• This stage produces approximately 32-34 molecules of ATP per glucose molecule.

subject: GK
question: When a host is exposed to antigens, which may be in the form of living or dead microbes or other proteins, antibodies are produced in the host body. This type of immunity is called ______ immunity.
solution:
The correct answer is __**active**__.

__
 
• **Vaccination** is another way to become immune to a disease. These ways of gaining immunity, either from having an illness or from vaccination, are examples of active immunity.
 
• Active immunity results when a person’s immune system works to produce antibodies and activate other** immune cells to certain pathogens**.
 
 
• If the person encounters that pathogen again, long-lasting immune cells specific to it will already be primed to fight it.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

__
 
• A different type of immunity, called** passive immunity**, results when a person is given someone else’s antibodies.

 
 
• Passive immunity is** "borrowed" **from another source and it lasts for a short time.
 
• For example, antibodies in a **mother's breast milk** give a baby temporary immunity to diseases the mother has been exposed to.
 
• When these antibodies are introduced into the person’s body, the “loaned” antibodies help prevent or fight certain infectious diseases.
 
• The protection offered by passive immunization is short-lived, usually lasting only a few weeks or months.
 
 
 
• **Adaptive (acquired) immunity**: This protects from pathogens that develop as we go through life.
 
 
• As we are exposed to diseases or get vaccinated, we build up a library of antibodies to different pathogens. This is sometimes referred to as **immunological memory** because our immune system remembers previous enemies.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **White blood cells** also called **leukocytes** (LOO-Kuh-sites), play an important role in the immune system.
 
• There are two main types of leukocyte:
 
 
• **Phagocytes**: These cells surround and absorb pathogens and break them down, effectively eating them.
 
• **Lymphocytes**: Lymphocytes help the body to remember previous invaders and recognize them if they come back to attack again.

question: Which protein is found in grains?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Gluten**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Gluten** is the main protein found in grains such as wheat, barley, and rye.
 
• It is a composite of storage proteins, namely gliadin and glutenin, which are conjoined with starch in the endosperm of various grass-related grains.
 
• Gluten gives dough its elasticity, helping it rise and keep its shape, and often gives the final product a chewy texture.
 
• While it is a common ingredient in many foods, some individuals have gluten intolerance or celiac disease, which requires them to follow a gluten-free diet.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Celiac disease** is an autoimmune disorder where ingestion of gluten leads to damage in the small intestine.
 
• A **gluten-free diet** involves excluding foods that contain gluten, which is found in wheat, barley, rye, and derivatives of these grains.
 
• Gluten-free products are widely available and are essential for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.
 
• Despite its necessity for some, a gluten-free diet is also adopted by others for various health benefits or lifestyle choices.

close the eyes through the eyelids to prevent damage to the lens from excessive light
process the information gathered by photoreceptor cells and send it to the brain to decide what the picture is
adjust the focus of the lens for formation of a clear image

solution:
The correct answer is __**option 3.**__

__
 
• The function of the retina is to **process the information gathered by photoreceptor cells and send them to the brain to decide what the picture is.**__
 
• The retina is located near the optic nerve and is a thin layer of tissue that lines the back of the eye on the inside.
 
• The **purpose of the retina is to receive light that the lens has focused, convert the light into neural signals, and send these signals on to the brain for visual recognition.**
 
• The retina is a complex transparent tissue consisting of several layers, only one of which contains light-sensitive photoreceptor cells.
 
• The light must pass through the overlying layers to reach the photoreceptor cells.

subject: GK
question:
Read the below statements about synaptic transmission:

1. Synaptic cleft is the gap between two neurons.

2. Neurotransmitters are released from presynaptic terminals.

3. Axon hillock receives impulses from the next neuron.

Which of the above statements are correct?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 1 and 2 are correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement 1:** Synaptic cleft is the gap between two neurons.

 
 
• The **synaptic cleft** is a small gap (usually around 20-40 nanometers wide) that exists between the **presynaptic neuron** and the **postsynaptic neuron**.
 
• This gap allows for the transmission of chemical signals (neurotransmitters) from one neuron to another.
 
• *Hence, statement 1 is correct.*
 
 
 
• **Statement 2:** Neurotransmitters are released from presynaptic terminals.
 
 
• Neurotransmitters are chemical messengers that are stored in vesicles located in the **axon terminals of the presynaptic neuron**.
 
• When an action potential reaches the presynaptic terminal, these neurotransmitters are released into the synaptic cleft via a process called **exocytosis**.
 
• The neurotransmitters then bind to specific receptors on the postsynaptic neuron, leading to signal transmission.
 
• *Hence, statement 2 is correct.*
 
 
 
• **Statement 3:** Axon hillock receives impulses from the next neuron.
 
 
• The **axon hillock** is the region of the neuron where the axon emerges from the cell body (soma). It is responsible for generating action potentials.
 
• However, it does not receive impulses from the next neuron. Instead, it integrates signals received by the dendrites and soma of the neuron.
 
• Signals from the **next neuron** are received by the **dendrites** or cell body via synapses.
 
• *Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.*
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Synapse:**

 
 
• A synapse is a junction between two neurons or between a neuron and a target cell (such as a muscle cell). It facilitates the transfer of signals.
 
• There are two types of synapses: **chemical synapses** (which involve neurotransmitters) and **electrical synapses** (which involve direct electrical communication).
 
 
 
• **Neurotransmitters:**
 
 
• These are chemical substances that transmit signals across the synaptic cleft. Examples include **acetylcholine**, **dopamine**, **serotonin**, and **glutamate**.
 
• Neurotransmitters can be excitatory (e.g., glutamate) or inhibitory (e.g., GABA).
 
 
 
• **Axon Hillock and Action Potential:**
 
 
• The axon hillock is the decision-making point of the neuron where the summation of excitatory and inhibitory signals determines whether an action potential will be generated.
 
• It is rich in voltage-gated sodium channels, which are essential for initiating the action potential.
 
 
 
• **Signal Transmission:**
 
 
• Neuronal communication involves the conversion of electrical signals into chemical signals and then back into electrical signals.
 
• This process ensures accurate and efficient signal relay across neurons in the nervous system.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The synaptic cleft ensures that signals are unidirectional, moving from the presynaptic neuron to the postsynaptic neuron.
 
• Neurotransmitters are stored in synaptic vesicles and released upon the arrival of an action potential.
 
• The postsynaptic neuron has specific receptors that determine the effect of the neurotransmitter (excitation or inhibition).
 
• Understanding synaptic transmission is crucial for studying brain functions, including learning, memory, and diseases like Parkinson’s or Alzheimer’s.

subject: GK
question: Why do pickles last longer?

options.text: Only beneficial bacteria can grow in the pickle.
The water content of the pickle protect the pickle from spoilage.
Pickle is prepared in a vacuum so that no harmful bacteria can grow on it.
Bacterial and fungal cells get plasmolysed in high salt concentration of pickle.

solution:
The Correct answer is__** Bacterial and fungal cells get plasmolysed in high salt concentrations of pickle.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Pickles **last longer primarily because of the high salt concentration used in their preparation, which causes bacterial and fungal cells to undergo** plasmolysis,** making the environment inhospitable for their growth. 
 
• During the pickling process, beneficial bacteria (such as **lactic acid bacteria**) play a crucial role.
 
• They ferment the sugars present in the vegetables, producing **lactic acid**. 
 
• This acidic environment inhibits the growth of harmful bacteria and preserves the pickle. So, while beneficial bacteria thrive, harmful ones are suppressed.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• When vegetables are submerged in a brine solution (which contains salt or vinegar), the high salt concentration draws water out of the cells through **osmosis**.
 
• The **reduced water availability prevents the growth of spoilage-causing microorganisms.**
 
• While **vacuum sealing **is used for certain types of pickles, it is not a universal method. 
 
• Vacuum-sealed pickles are prepared in an **environment devoid of oxygen**, preventing the growth of aerobic bacteria and molds.
 
• However, most pickles rely on the natural fermentation process rather than vacuum sealing.

question: Which bacteria have a thick cell wall with several layers of peptidoglycan and teichoic acid?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Staphylococcus aureus**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Staphylococcus aureus** has a thick cell wall composed of several layers of peptidoglycan and teichoic acid.
 
• The thick peptidoglycan layer provides structural strength and rigidity to the bacterial cell wall.
 
• Teichoic acid, which is embedded in the cell wall, plays a role in cell wall maintenance and ion regulation.
 
• These features are characteristic of **Gram-positive bacteria**, to which Staphylococcus aureus belongs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Salmonella enterica**, **Pseudomonas aeruginosa**, and **Escherichia coli** are examples of **Gram-negative bacteria**, which have a thinner peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane.
 
• Gram-positive bacteria, like Staphylococcus aureus, stain violet in the Gram staining procedure due to their thick peptidoglycan layer.
 
• The structure of the cell wall in Gram-positive bacteria makes them more susceptible to certain antibiotics, such as penicillin, which targets peptidoglycan synthesis.

subject: GK
question: Identify the reason for formation of dental plaque.

options.text: When acids stick to the teeth
Masses of bacterial cells together with food particles stick to the teeth
When bacteria acting on sugars produce acids

solution:
The correct answer is __**Masses of bacterial cells together with food particles stick to the teeth**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Masses of bacterial cells together with food particles stick to the teeth** are the primary reason for the formation of dental plaque.
 
• Dental plaque is a sticky, colorless or pale yellow film that is constantly forming on your teeth.
 
• Plaque is made up of bacteria and food particles. When you consume foods or drinks that contain sugars or starches, the bacteria in plaque produce acids that attack tooth enamel.
 
• If plaque is not removed by regular brushing and flossing, it can harden into tartar (calculus), which can lead to gum disease and cavities.
 
• Maintaining good oral hygiene by brushing twice a day, flossing daily, and visiting the dentist regularly can help prevent the formation of plaque and tartar.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Saliva** helps to wash away food particles and neutralize acids produced by bacteria in the mouth, which helps to protect against plaque buildup.
 
• **Fluoride**, found in many dental products and drinking water, helps to strengthen tooth enamel and prevent decay.
 
• **Regular dental check-ups** can help identify and treat plaque and tartar buildup before it leads to more serious dental issues.
 
• Some **foods and beverages**, such as sugary snacks and drinks, can contribute to plaque formation and should be consumed in moderation.
 
• Using **antibacterial mouthwash** can also help reduce the number of bacteria in the mouth that contribute to plaque formation.

question: Nuclear membrane is absent in organisms that fall under kingdom ______.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Monera**__.

__
 
• A **prokaryote** is a relatively **simple single-celled organism**.

 
 
• **Only one kingdom of prokaryotes, known as Monera**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Whittaker** proposed an elaborate **five-kingdom classification – Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia**.
 
• **Carl Woese** proposed **six-kingdom classification - Animalia, Plantae, Fungi, Protista, Archaea/Archaebacteria, and Bacteria/Eubacteria.**
 
• In the six-kingdom classification, **Monera was divided into two parts Archaea and Eubacteria**.

 
 

 
 
MONERA (EUBACTERIA & ARCHAEA)

 
 
 
 
• Prokaryotic, unicellular organisms.
 
• No cell nucleus nor any other membrane-bound organelles within their cells.
 
 
 
 

 
 
PROTISTA

 
 
 
 
• Eukaryotic cells with nucleus, enclosed by a membrane.
 
• It includes slime molds, Euglenoids, protozoans, etc.
 
 
 
 

 
 
FUNGI

 
 
 
 
• Multicellular, with a cell wall, organelles including a nucleus, but no chloroplasts.
 
• They have no mechanisms for locomotion.
 
 
 
 

 
 
PLANTAE

 
 
 
 
• Multicellular form with specialized eukaryotic cells.
 
• Do not have their own means of locomotion.
 
• It includes algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms.
 
 
 
 

 
 
ANIMALIA

 
 
 
 
• Multicellular form with specialized eukaryotic cells.
 
• They have their own means of locomotion.

• **It is a genus of single-celled green algae that are found in freshwater and marine habitats around the world. **
 
• They are known for their flagella, which they use for movement, and their ability to photosynthesize.
 
• Chlamydomonas are also important for their role in the nitrogen cycle and their potential for use in biofuel production.
 
 
 
• **Fucus:-**
 
 
• **It is a genus of brown algae that are found in intertidal zones around the world. **
 
• They are known for their large, leafy bodies and their ability to withstand harsh conditions.
 
• Fucus are an important food source for marine invertebrates and are also used as a fertilizer and a source of alginates.
 
 
 
• **Nostoc:-**
 
 
• **It is a genus of filamentous cyanobacteria that are found in freshwater and terrestrial habitats around the world. **
 
• They are known for their ability to fix nitrogen, a process that converts atmospheric nitrogen into a form that can be used by plants and other organisms.
 
• Nostoc are also an important food source for some animals and are used in traditional Chinese medicine.

subject: GK
question: The structure that produces and holds sperm cells in bryophytes (non-vascular plants) and ferns is called:
solution:
The correct answer is __**antheridium**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Antheridium:-**

 
 
• **The structure that produces and holds sperm cells in bryophytes (non-vascular plants) and ferns is called an antheridium.**
 
• It is a small, multicellular structure that typically consists of a jacket of sterile cells surrounding a cluster of sperm cells.
 
• The sperm cells, also known as antherozoids, are flagellated, meaning they have tails that allow them to swim.
 
• When the antheridium matures, the jacket ruptures, releasing the sperm cells into the surrounding water.
 
• The sperm cells then swim towards the archegonia, which are the structures that produce egg cells in bryophytes and ferns. 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Megasporangia:-**

 
 
• **These are structures that produce megaspores, which are large, haploid spores that develop into female gametophytes. **
 
• Female gametophytes are the haploid phase of the plant life cycle and produce egg cells.
 
• Megasporangia are typically found on the sporophytes, which are the diploid phase of the plant life cycle and produce spores.
 
 
 
• **Archegonia:-**
 
 
• These are structures that produce egg cells.
 
• **They are also found on the gametophytes. Archegonia are typically flask-shaped and have a neck, a venter, and an egg cell. **
 
• When a sperm cell swims down the neck of an archegonium and fertilizes the egg cell, a zygote is formed. The zygote develops into a sporophyte.
 
 
 
• **Protonema:-**
 
 
• It is the first stage of the life cycle of a non-vascular plant.
 
• **It is a filamentous, thread-like structure that develops from a germinating spore. **
 
• The protonema is responsible for anchorage and absorption of water and nutrients. It also produces buds that develop into gametophytes.

subject: GK
question: Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The transport of male gametes in Gymnosperms occurs through water.
The transport of male gametes in bryophytes and pteridophytes occurs through water.
The transport of male gametes in bryophytes and pteridophytes occurs through air.
The transport of male gametes in angiosperms occurs through water.

solution:
The correct answer is __**The transport of male gametes in bryophytes and pteridophytes occurs through water**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Male gametes** in **both bryophytes and pteridophytes **rely on** water for transportation**.
 
• Produced within antheridia, these male gametes are liberated as free-swimming sperm cells equipped with flagella, enabling them to move through water.
 
• Once released, they navigate to the female reproductive organs for fertilization. Water plays a vital role in the life cycle of bryophytes and pteridophytes, as it facilitates the movement of male gametes.
 
• This dependency on water for reproduction leads to the classification of bryophytes as amphibians of the plant kingdom, emphasizing their need for aquatic environments to complete their life cycle. 
 
• Bryophytes and pteridophytes typically thrive in environments characterized by dampness, shade, and humidity, often found in close proximity to water bodies.
 
• In such habitats, these plants rely on water as a conduit for the movement of their male gametes from the antheridium (male reproductive organ) to the archegonium (female reproductive organ).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Bryophytes** represent a category of land plants, often regarded as a distinct taxonomic division. This group encompasses three main types of non-vascular land plants: liverworts, hornworts, and mosses. Despite lacking vascular tissues for efficient water and nutrient transport, bryophytes play crucial ecological roles in various ecosystems.
 
• **Pteridophytes** are vascular plants that reproduce via spores rather than seeds. They earned the moniker "cryptogams" due to their method of reproduction, which occurs inconspicuously. Pteridophytes include ferns, horsetails, and clubmosses, among others, and they play significant roles in both terrestrial and aquatic habitats.

question: Identify the third germinal layer found in triploblastic animals.
solution:
The correct answer is **__Mesoderm__**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The third germinal** layer found in triploblastic animals is the **mesoderm**.
 
• The mesoderm, positioned between the ectoderm and endoderm, is the middle layer among the three germ layers formed during gastrulation in early embryo development across most animals.
 
• It gives rise to various structures such as mesenchyme, mesothelium, non-epithelial blood cells, and coelomocytes.
 
• Mesothelium lines coeloms, while mesoderm contributes to the formation of muscles through myogenesis, as well as septa and mesenteries.
 
• Additionally, it plays a role in forming parts of the gonads, with myogenesis specifically driven by mesenchyme.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The ectoderm,** positioned as the outermost layer among the three primary germ layers, develops during early embryonic development. It lies superficially to the mesoderm (the middle layer) and the endoderm (the innermost layer).
 
• **A coelom** serves as a fluid-filled cavity that shields the internal organs of numerous organisms, functioning as the body cavity in animals.
 
• **Endoderm, **constituting the innermost layer of the embryo, contributes to the formation of the digestive tract and various other bodily structures.

• **Adult female Ascaris worms** can reach lengths exceeding one foot, while adult males typically measure between 15 to 30 centimeters.

• **Liver fluke** refers to a group of parasitic flatworms, known as trematodes, which infect the livers of various mammals, including humans.
 
• **Taenia** is a genus of tapeworms that encompasses more than 100 species, responsible for causing cysticercosis and taeniasis in humans.

question: To what phylum does a blood sucking leech belong?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Annelida**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

• Leeches belong to the phylum **Annelida**.
 
• Annelida is a phylum of segmented worms, which also includes earthworms and polychaetes.
 
• Leeches are characterized by their segmented bodies and the presence of suckers at both ends, which they use for attachment and feeding.
 
• They are mostly found in freshwater environments, but some species are terrestrial or marine.
 
• Leeches are known for their role in medicine, particularly in ancient times and even today in microsurgery for their blood-sucking capabilities and anticoagulant properties.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• In modern medicine, leeches are sometimes used in reconstructive surgery to help stimulate blood circulation in reattached tissues.
 
• Leeches produce a substance called hirudin, which is a powerful anticoagulant, preventing blood from clotting during feeding.
 
• The study of annelids is important in understanding soil health and ecosystem dynamics, as many annelids play crucial roles in soil aeration and nutrient cycling.

subject: GK
question: Which of the following organisms can initiate ecological succession even in bare rocks?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Lichens.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Lichens are considered **pioneer species**, meaning they are among the first organisms to colonize bare rocks.
 
• Lichens secrete acids that slowly **break down rocks**, leading to the formation of soil, making it possible for other plants to grow.
 
• Lichens consist of fungi and algae (or cyanobacteria) living in a **symbiotic relationship**, allowing them to survive in harsh conditions.
 
• They are extremely** resilient** and can survive in extreme **environmental conditions**, such as high altitudes and exposed rock surfaces.
 
• **Soil formation:** By breaking down rock and accumulating organic material, lichens contribute to the creation of the first layer of soil.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__****Orchids:**

 
• Orchids often grow on **other plants** (such as trees) without harming them, known as epiphytes, and are not capable of growing directly on bare rocks.
 
• Orchids typically appear in more advanced stages of **ecological succession** when the environment is more hospitable, with developed soil and host plants.
 
• They thrive in humid environments with specific light, moisture, and nutrient conditions, relying on **organic material** rather than barren environments.

**Aspergillus:**

 
• Aspergillus is a genus of **fungi **that decomposes organic matter and grows in a variety of environments, but it does not colonize bare rocks.
 
• This fungus breaks down already existing **organic matter**, such as dead plants or animals, and is more common in later stages of succession.
 
• Certain species of Aspergillus can cause **diseases** in plants and animals, including humans (e.g., aspergillosis in humans).

**Lily:**

 
• Lilies are **angiosperms** (flowering plants) that require a developed soil layer rich in nutrients, water, and light to grow.
 
• They appear in ecosystems where soil formation has already occurred, indicating that they are not **pioneer** species.
 
• Lilies grow in **wetlands** or well-drained, nutrient-rich soils and cannot survive in barren or rocky environments.

subject: GK
question:
Arrange these evolutionary events chronologically:

A. First eukaryotes

B. First prokaryotes

C. Multicellularity

D. Oxygen accumulation
solution:
The correct answer is __**1) B-D-A-C**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **B. First prokaryotes:** The earliest forms of life on Earth were prokaryotic cells, which appeared approximately 3.5 to 3.8 billion years ago. These were simple, unicellular organisms without a nucleus.
 
• **D. Oxygen accumulation:** Prokaryotes, such as cyanobacteria, were responsible for the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE) around 2.5 billion years ago. This event led to the accumulation of oxygen in Earth's atmosphere.
 
• **A. First eukaryotes:** Eukaryotic cells, which are more complex with a defined nucleus, evolved approximately 1.8 billion years ago. This advancement allowed for more specialized cellular functions.
 
• **C. Multicellularity:** Multicellular organisms emerged around 600 million years ago, enabling the formation of complex life forms with specialized tissues and organs.
 
• The correct chronological order of these evolutionary events is **B-D-A-C:** First prokaryotes → Oxygen accumulation → First eukaryotes → Multicellularity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Prokaryotes:**
 
 
• Prokaryotes are single-celled organisms without a membrane-bound nucleus or organelles.
 
• Bacteria and archaea are the two domains of prokaryotes.
 
• They played a crucial role in shaping early Earth's environment, including the production of oxygen through photosynthesis.
 
 
 
• **Oxygen Accumulation (Great Oxygenation Event):**
 
 
• The Great Oxygenation Event was a dramatic increase in Earth's atmospheric oxygen levels due to photosynthetic activity by cyanobacteria.
 
• This event was critical for the evolution of aerobic (oxygen-dependent) life forms.
 
• It also caused the first mass extinction by eliminating many anaerobic organisms that could not survive in oxygen-rich environments.
 
 
 
• **Eukaryotes:**
 
 
• Eukaryotic cells are characterized by a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles such as mitochondria and chloroplasts.
 
• The endosymbiotic theory explains their evolution, suggesting that eukaryotic cells arose through the symbiosis of different prokaryotic cells.
 
• Eukaryotes include plants, animals, fungi, and protists.
 
 
 
• **Multicellularity:**
 
 
• Multicellularity allowed organisms to develop specialized cells for different functions, such as muscle cells, nerve cells, and blood cells.
 
• This advancement led to the evolution of complex life forms, including plants and animals.
 
• Examples of early multicellular organisms include algae and simple sponges.

• Algae

question: The charge has to be passed ______ to obtain maximum work from a galvanic cell.
solution:
The correct answer is __**reversibly**__.

__
 
• There are** two types** of electrochemical cells: **galvanic, also called Voltaic, and electrolytic**.

 
 
• **Galvanic** cells derive their energy from **spontaneous redox reactions**.
 
• **Electrolytic** cells involve **non-spontaneous reactions **and thus require an external electron source like a DC battery or an AC power source.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• Galvanic cells traditionally are used as sources of **DC electrical power**.
 
• **Oxidation occurs at the anode and reduction occurs at the cathode**. Since the reaction at the anode is the source of electrons for the current, the anode is the negative terminal for the galvanic cell.
 
• The maximum work of a galvanic cell is **equal to Gibb's free energy of the cell**.
 
 
• Only happen when the cell is used **reversibly**.
 
• **The reversible work done by a galvanic cell is equal to a decrease in its Gibbs energy**.

question: Bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances. This process is called as ______.
solution:
The correct answer is __**catabolism**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances. This process is called as catabolism.
 
• The word **catabolism is from New Latin**, which got the roots from Greek: **κάτω Kato, "downward"** and** βάλλειν ballein**, "to throw".
 
• It breaks down large molecules like **polysaccharides, lipids, etc. into smaller units like monosaccharides, fatty acids, nucleotides, etc**.
 
• It is the breaking-down aspect of **metabolism**.
 
• Cells use the monomers released from breaking down polymers to either construct new polymer molecules or degrade them into simple waste products like **lactic acid, carbon dioxide, acetic acid, urea, and ammonia, releasing energy**.
 
• The creation of these wastes is usually an oxidation process involving a release of chemical-free energy. Of this, some are lost as heat, and the rest results in the formation of adenosine triphosphate (ATP).​

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Catabolism** is a metabolic process in which complex molecules are broken down into simpler ones with the release of energy. In the context of the given statement, bacterial and fungal enzymes break down the complex detritus into simpler inorganic substances such as carbon dioxide, water, and mineral ions. This breakdown process releases energy that can be used by the decomposers or other organisms in the ecosystem.
 
• Fragmentation: Detritivores (e.g., earthworms) break down detritus into smaller particles. This process is called fragmentation.
 
• Leaching: By the process of leaching, water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts.
 
• Decomposition: It** **is the process of breaking down a substance into its constituent parts. Decomposition of dead organic matter occurs in nature and it is also called decay or putrefaction.​

question: Which of the following is NOT the manifestation of Iron-deficiency anaemia (IDA)?
solution:
The correct answer is__** Blindness**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Iron deficiency anemia (IDA)** manifests in various ways, but one of the** not** commonly associated manifestations is **blindness.**
 
• Other conditions (such as** vitamin A deficiency** or specific **eye diseases**) can cause blindness, but they are not directly related to IDA.
 
• **Symptoms of IDA:**
 
 
• **Extreme Fatigue:** Individuals with IDA often experience severe tiredness and weakness.
 
• **Pale Skin:** The skin may appear unusually pale due to reduced hemoglobin levels.
 
• **Cold Hands and Feet:** Poor circulation can lead to cold extremities.
 
• **Brittle Nails:** IDA affects nail health, causing them to become brittle.
 
• **Inflammation or Soreness of the Tongue:** Known as glossitis, this condition can occur.
 
• **Unusual Cravings for Non-Nutritive Substances:** Some people with IDA crave ice, dirt, or starch (a condition **called pica**).
 
• **Poor Appetite in Infants and Children: **Children with IDA may have reduced appetite.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**** Soft Palate:**

 
• The** soft palate** is the fleshy part at the back of the roof of the mouth.
 
• In IDA, the soft palate may appear pale due to reduced hemoglobin levels.
 
• This paleness is a result of decreased oxygen-carrying capacity in the blood.

**General Pallor:**

 
• **General pallor** refers to the overall paleness of the skin.
 
• It is a common sign of IDA due to reduced red blood cell production.
 
• The skin, mucous membranes, and conjunctiva (lining of the eyes) may all appear pale.

**Paleness of Conjunctiva of Eyes:**

 
• **The conjunctiva** is the thin, transparent layer covering the white part of the eye.
 
• In IDA, the conjunctiva may appear pale (a condition called conjunctival pallor).
 
• **Anemia **affects the blood vessels in the conjunctiva, leading to paleness.

• **Ribosomes** are the only organelles found in both eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells.

• Ribosomes can be found floating freely within the cytoplasm or attached to the endoplasmic reticulum in eukaryotic cells.

• **Eukaryotic cells** contain various membrane-bound organelles, including the nucleus, mitochondria, and lysosomes, which are absent in prokaryotic cells.
 
• The presence of ribosomes in both cell types highlights their essential role in the fundamental process of protein synthesis.
 
• The differences in ribosome size between prokaryotes and eukaryotes are due to variations in their ribosomal RNA and protein content.

question: Identify the structure that controls the size of the pupil.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Iris.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The** iris** controls the **size of the pupil** by adjusting its diameter through the contraction and dilation of its muscles, regulating the amount of light entering the eye.
 
• The iris is the colored part of the eye, with its color varying due to the amount and type of** pigment** present. This color can be blue, brown, green, etc.
 
• It consists of two sets of smooth muscles: the **sphincter pupillae** (which constricts the pupil) and the **dilator pupillae** (which dilates the pupil).
 
• The iris plays a** crucial** role in adapting to different lighting conditions by controlling pupil size, helping to protect the retina from excessive light, and improving vision in varying light conditions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Vitreous Humour:**

 
 
• A gel-like substance fills the space between the **lens** and the **retina**.
 
• It helps maintain the** eye’s shape **and provides a pathway for light to reach the retina.
 
• It does not play a role in controlling pupil size or light regulation.
 
 
 
• **Ciliary Muscles:**
 
 
• **Muscles** located around the lens of the eye.
 
• They control the shape of the lens for focusing on near and distant objects (accommodation).
 
• While **crucial for focusing**, they do not control pupil size.
 
 
 
• **Cornea:**
 
 
• The transparent, outer layer of the eye that covers the** iris **and** pupil**.
 
• It provides most of the eye's **optical power** by refracting light entering the eye.
 
• It does not control the size of the pupil; rather, it helps **focus light **on the retina.
