__
 
• In India, the **long-term plans **that delineate specific objectives to be achieved over five years and 20 years are referred to as** perspective plans.**
 
• These plans enable adjustments in funding and projects to align with the nation's economic requirements.
 
• **Economic planning** in India entails the government's formulation of long-term strategies to develop and coordinate the economy efficiently.
 
• The first five-year plan was initiated in **1951**, marking the inception of India's planned development approach. Since then, the country has implemented twelve such plans.
 
• **The Planning Commission and the NITI Aayog** are responsible for devising, executing, and monitoring these plans.
 
• **The Prime Minister** serves as the** ex-officio chairman,** while the commission includes a nominated Deputy Chairman with the rank of a cabinet minister.
 
• The overarching objectives of the Five-Year Plans encompass achieving a high growth rate to enhance living standards, ensuring economic stability for prosperity, fostering a self-reliant economy, promoting social justice and reducing inequalities, and modernizing the economy to meet contemporary needs.

• **From 1947 to 2017, **the Indian economy operated on the basis of planned development, which was facilitated through the implementation of **Five-Year Plans.**
 
• These plans were formulated, executed, and monitored by the Planning Commission from **1951 to 2014**, and subsequently by the** NITI Aayog** from **2015 to 2017.**
 
• The Prime Minister served as the ex-officio chairman of these commissions, while a nominated Deputy Chairman, holding the rank of a cabinet minister, assisted in their operations. Montek Singh Ahluwalia served as the** last Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission,** resigning on **May 26, 2014.**

question: What was the target growth rate of the Indian economy in the second five-year plan?
solution:
The correct answer is **__4.5%__**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The second five-year plan, **spanning from **1956 to 1961, **aimed for a **target growth rate **of** 4.5% **for the Indian economy.
 
• However, the actual growth rate fell slightly short at **4.27%**.
 
• **Drafted by P.C. Mahalanobis**, this plan prioritized rapid industrialization and the development of the public sector, with an emphasis on achieving quick structural transformation.
 
• To protect domestic industries, the government implemented tariffs on imports, while also allocating nearly 50 billion rupees across various sectors to meet set targets.
 
• Additionally, the plan advocated for the adoption of new technology and efficient investments to propel India's annual national income growth.
 
• Despite its objectives, the second five-year plan faced criticism from classical liberal economist **B.R. Shenoy**.
 
• He argued that the plan's heavy reliance on deficit financing to promote industrialization posed significant risks and could potentially lead to economic instability.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The Second Five-Year Plan** placed a significant emphasis on the development of the public sector and aimed for **"rapid industrialization."**
 
• This plan was guided by the **Mahalanobis model,** an economic development framework devised by Indian statistician Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis in 1953.
 
• At the core of the plan was the objective of determining the optimal allocation of investment across various productive sectors to achieve maximum long-term economic growth.
 
• To achieve this, the plan utilized state-of-the-art techniques of operations research and optimization, along with innovative applications of statistical models developed at the Indian Statistical Institute.

• The Minimum Needs Programme introduced in the first year of this plan, aimed to provide basic minimum needs.
 
• **MNP was prepared by D.P. Dhar.**
 
• The **target growth rate was 4.4%** and the** actual growth rate turned out to be 4.8%**
 
• In 1978, the newly elected **Morarji Desai **government rejected this plan.

**Eighth Five Year Plan (1992-97) - **

 
• The Eighth Plan promoted the **modernisation of Industries.**
 
• **India became a member of the World Trade Organisation on 1 January 1995.**
 
• The goals were to control population growth, reduce poverty, generate employment, strengthen the development of infrastructure, manage tourism, focus on human resource development etc.
 
• It also laid emphasis on involving the Panchayats and Nagar Palikas through decentralisation.
 
• The** target growth rate was 5.6%** but the **actual growth rate was an incredible 6.8%.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The idea of **five-year plans **is simple- The Government of India prepares a document with all its income and expenditure for five years.
 
• The budget of the central government and all the state governments is divided into two parts: **non-plan budget and plan budget.**
 
• The non-plan budget is spent on routine items yearly. The planned budget is spent on a five-year basis as per the priorities fixed by the plan.
 
• The model of the** Indian Economy **was premised on the concept of planning based on five-year plans from **1951-2017.**
 
• The Five Year Plans were formulated, implemented and regulated by a body known as the Planning Commission.
 
• The Planning Commission was replaced by a think tank called** NITI AAYOG in 2015.**
 
• The **Niti Aayog **has come out with three documents — 3-year action agenda, 7-year medium-term strategy paper and 15-year vision document.

question: Which of the folowing statements shows accurate understanding of a macroeconomic concept?

options.text: Gross Domestic Product includes earnings sent home by citizens working abroad.
When the general price level rises, the value of money tends to fall.
A country's budget is considered balanced when exports exceed imports.
The central bank controls inflation mainly through changes in income tax rates.

solution:
The correct answer is __**When the general price level rises, the value of money tends to fall**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• When the general price level in an economy rises, it leads to inflation, which reduces the purchasing power of money.
 
• This means that with the same amount of money, people can buy fewer goods and services as prices increase.
 
• The phenomenon is explained by the **inverse relationship between the value of money and price levels**: as prices increase, the value of money decreases.
 
• The value of money is often measured in terms of the quantity of goods and services it can purchase (real value).
 
• This concept is critical for understanding inflation and its effects on savings, investments, and the overall economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: Gross Domestic Product includes earnings sent home by citizens working abroad.**
 
 
• This is incorrect because Gross Domestic Product (GDP) only includes the value of goods and services produced within a country’s borders.
 
• Earnings sent home by citizens working abroad are classified under **Gross National Income (GNI)** or Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA), not GDP.
 
• GDP focuses solely on domestic economic activity, regardless of who owns the production factors.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: A country's budget is considered balanced when exports exceed imports.**
 
 
• This statement is incorrect as it confuses the concept of a **trade surplus** with a balanced budget.
 
• A balanced budget refers to a government’s fiscal position where its revenue equals its expenditure, not trade balances.
 
• A trade surplus occurs when a country’s exports exceed its imports, but it is unrelated to a government’s budget.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: The central bank controls inflation mainly through changes in income tax rates.**
 
 
• This is incorrect because income tax rates are determined by the government, not the central bank.
 
• The central bank primarily controls inflation through **monetary policy tools**, such as adjusting interest rates (repo rate), open market operations, and controlling the money supply.
 
• Fiscal tools like income tax rates are part of the government’s policy, not the central bank’s function.

__

• **Option 3: A is true but R is false**

• **Option 4: A is false but R is true**
 
 
• This option is incorrect because the Assertion (A) is true; the Third Five Year Plan did fail to meet its targets.

• Its failure highlighted the challenges posed by external factors and the need for effective contingency planning in economic policy-making.

question: Which year marked the beginning of India's First Five-Year Plan?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1951**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **First Five-Year Plan** in India was launched in the year **1951**. It was a landmark initiative aimed at the economic development of the country post-independence.
 
• The plan was introduced by the then Prime Minister, **Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru**, and it primarily focused on **agriculture, irrigation, and energy** production.
 
• The First Five-Year Plan covered the period from **1951 to 1956**, laying the foundation for planned economic development in India.
 
• The plan was based on the **Harrod-Domar model**, which emphasized capital investment to promote growth.
 
• With a total outlay of **2,069 crore INR**, the plan allocated the majority of funds to **irrigation and agriculture (31%)**, reflecting the agrarian economy of the country during that era.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Objectives of the First Five-Year Plan:**

 
 
• The primary goal was to boost **agriculture production** to ensure food self-sufficiency in the country.
 
• It aimed to improve **infrastructure, including transportation, energy, and irrigation facilities**, for economic development.
 
• Emphasis was also placed on **poverty reduction** and improving living standards.
 
 
 
• **Harrod-Domar Model:**
 
 
• This economic model formed the basis of the First Five-Year Plan in India and focused on the relationship between growth, savings, and investment.
 
• It suggested that economic growth could be achieved by increasing the rate of investment and the productivity of capital.
 
 
 
• **Achievements of the First Five-Year Plan:**
 
 
• There was a significant improvement in **agricultural production**, with India achieving self-sufficiency in food grains for the first time.
 
• Major irrigation projects like the **Bhakra-Nangal Dam** and the **Hirakud Dam** were initiated.
 
• Infrastructure development and increased industrial production were notable outcomes of the plan.
 
 
 
• **Other Five-Year Plans:**
 
 
• The **Second Five-Year Plan (1956–1961)** focused on industrialization and was based on the **Mahalanobis model**.
 
• Subsequent plans targeted various aspects of development like education, health, and rural development.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Significance of Five-Year Plans:**

 
 
• They were instrumental in shaping India's **economic policies** and driving growth in key sectors.
 
• Helped establish a planned and centralized approach to development under the **Planning Commission** (now replaced by the **NITI Aayog**).
 
 
 
• **Key Facts:**
 
 
• The **Planning Commission** was set up in **1950** to formulate and execute Five-Year Plans in India.
 
• The Five-Year Plans were inspired by the **Soviet Union's model** of economic planning.

question: Which of the following best describes the concept of 'opportunity cost' in microeconomics?

options.text: The cost of producing goods in the future
The net gain from an investment
The value of the best alternative forgone

solution:
The correct answer is __**The value of the best alternative forgone**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Opportunity cost** is a fundamental concept in microeconomics, referring to the value of the next best alternative that is forgone when a decision is made.
 
• It emphasizes the idea that every choice involves a trade-off where resources could be allocated differently for potentially greater benefits.
 
• It is not just about monetary costs but encompasses any benefit or value that is given up, such as time, effort, or utility.
 
• For example, if a person chooses to spend money on a vacation instead of investing it, the opportunity cost is the potential returns from the investment that they forego.
 
• This concept is crucial for decision-making, as it helps individuals and businesses evaluate the relative benefits and costs of alternative options, thereby optimizing resource allocation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Characteristics of Opportunity Cost:**

 
 
• It is subjective, varying based on individual priorities, circumstances, and preferences.
 
• It considers both explicit costs (direct monetary expenses) and implicit costs (non-monetary sacrifices).
 
• Opportunity cost is often applied in various fields such as economics, business, and personal finance.
 
• It plays a key role in production decisions, such as determining the allocation of resources among competing goods and services.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Opportunity Cost:**
 
 
• In business, companies use opportunity cost to decide between investment projects, production methods, or market strategies.
 
• Opportunity cost is also applied in daily life decisions, such as choosing between leisure activities and work or saving versus spending.
 
• Governments consider opportunity costs when allocating budgets across sectors like education, healthcare, and defense.
 
 
 
• **Examples:**
 
 
• Choosing to attend college involves opportunity costs such as lost earnings from full-time work during that period.
 
• Farmers deciding between growing wheat or corn face an opportunity cost in terms of the potential profit from the crop they forego.
 
• Investors selecting one stock over another incur opportunity costs if the forgone stock performs better.
 
 
 
• **Important Economic Context:**
 
 
• The concept of opportunity cost is tied to the idea of scarcity, as resources are limited, and choices must be made.
 
• It is closely related to the production possibility frontier (PPF), which illustrates trade-offs and opportunity costs in resource allocation.
 
• Opportunity cost is central to cost-benefit analysis, helping to weigh the potential gains and losses of decisions.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Option 1: The cost of producing goods in the future**

 
 
• This option is incorrect because opportunity cost relates to the best alternative forgone, not the future cost of production.
 
 
 
• **Option 2: The net gain from an investment**
 
 
• This option is incorrect as opportunity cost assesses the value of the next best alternative, not the direct financial gain from an investment.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: The value of leisure forgone**
 
 
• While leisure forgone can be an example of opportunity cost, this option does not fully encompass the broader concept.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: The value of the best alternative forgone**
 
 
• This is the correct option as it accurately describes opportunity cost, emphasizing the trade-offs involved in decision-making.

• The plan emphasized **Food, Work, and Productivity**, aiming to increase efficiency in the **private sector** while reducing the absolute dominance of the public sector.
 
• For the first time in Indian planning history, the **private sector** was given priority over the public sector in terms of investment outlays, creating a precursor to the **Market Economy**.

question: When is total revenue maximized in relation to elasticity?

options.text: When elasticity is greater than one
When elasticity is less than one
When marginal cost equals marginal revenue

solution:
The correct answer is __**When elasticity equals one**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Total Revenue (TR)** is the total amount of money a firm receives from selling its goods or services, calculated as **Price (P) × Quantity (Q)**.
 
• **Price Elasticity of Demand (PED)** measures the responsiveness of the quantity demanded of a good to a change in its price. When the **absolute value of elasticity** is exactly **1**, it is known as **Unitary Elasticity**.
 
• The relationship between **Marginal Revenue (MR)** and elasticity is expressed by the formula: **MR = P × (1 − 1/|e|)**. When elasticity **|e| = 1**, the **Marginal Revenue** becomes **zero**.
 
• In calculus, the maximum point of a function (Total Revenue) occurs when its first derivative (Marginal Revenue) is **zero**. Therefore, **Total Revenue** reaches its peak at the point where the demand curve is **unit elastic**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **When elasticity is greater than one (Elastic Demand):**

 
 
• A decrease in price leads to a proportionately larger increase in quantity demanded, causing **Total Revenue** to rise.
 
• In this range, **Marginal Revenue** is **positive**.
 
 
 
• **When elasticity is less than one (Inelastic Demand):**
 
 
• A decrease in price leads to a proportionately smaller increase in quantity demanded, causing **Total Revenue** to fall.
 
• In this range, **Marginal Revenue** is **negative**.
 
 
 
• **When marginal cost equals marginal revenue:**
 
 
• This is the condition for **Profit Maximization** rather than **Revenue Maximization**.
 
• A **Rational Producer** aims to produce at the level where the additional cost of the last unit equals the additional revenue gained, ensuring the highest net profit.

question:
Read the following statements and select the appropriate options:

**Statement 1:** A budget deficit is encountered when the total expenditure of the government is greater than its total revenue, excluding borrowings.

**Statement 2:** A budget deficit is faced when the total revenue of the government is greater than its expenditure in a fiscal year.

options.text: Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are correct

solution:
The correct answer is __**Only Statement 1 is correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement 1:** A budget deficit is encountered when the **total expenditure of the government exceeds its total revenue, excluding borrowings**. This definition aligns with the economic concept of a budget deficit. *Hence, Statement 1 is correct.*
 
• **Statement 2:** This statement incorrectly reverses the concept of a budget deficit. If the total revenue of the government is greater than its expenditure, it results in a budget surplus, not a deficit. *Hence, Statement 2 is incorrect.*
 
• A **budget deficit** occurs when the government’s expenditure on services, infrastructure, and other public sector needs surpasses its revenue collections (excluding borrowing).
 
• A common source of revenue for governments includes **taxation, non-tax revenues, and dividends**, whereas expenditures include welfare programs, salaries, interest payments, and infrastructure spending.
 
• To cover a budget deficit, governments often rely on borrowing, which may take the form of issuing bonds or loans from domestic and international markets.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Types of Budget Deficits:**

 
 
• **Revenue Deficit:** It occurs when the government’s total revenue receipts are less than its revenue expenditures.
 
• **Fiscal Deficit:** This is the total borrowing requirement of the government. It is calculated as the difference between total expenditure and total receipts (excluding borrowings).
 
• **Primary Deficit:** This is the fiscal deficit excluding interest payments on previous borrowings. It reflects the current year's borrowing needs.
 
 
 
• **Impacts of a Budget Deficit:**
 
 
• Governments may resort to borrowing, leading to an increase in public debt.
 
• Excessive deficits can lead to inflation if financed by printing money.
 
• In the long term, persistent deficits may lead to economic instability.
 
 
 
• **Budget Surplus:** A budget surplus occurs when the government’s total revenue exceeds its total expenditure in a fiscal year. This allows governments to reduce debt or invest in infrastructure.
 
• **Examples:**
 
 
• India often reports fiscal deficits in its Union Budget, reflecting the need for borrowing to fund development and welfare programs.
 
• Countries such as Germany and Switzerland have occasionally achieved budget surpluses due to high revenues and controlled expenditures.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Government Budget:** A government budget is an annual financial statement presenting its anticipated revenue and expenditure for the coming fiscal year.
 
• **Fiscal Responsibility:** Governments adopt fiscal responsibility laws, such as the **Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003,** in India, to ensure fiscal discipline.
 
• **Balanced Budget:** In a balanced budget, government revenues are equal to expenditures. While rare, such budgets are considered fiscally ideal for long-term stability.

question: Which of the following Five-Year Plans marked a strategic transition in India's economic policy, shifting the primary focus from agriculture to the development of heavy industries and industrialization?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Second Five-Year Plan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Second Five-Year Plan** (1956-1961) marked a **strategic shift in India's economic policy**, emphasizing the development of heavy industries and industrialization over agriculture.
 
• This plan was based on the **Mahalnobis Model**, which prioritized industrialization and aimed at building the foundation of a self-reliant economy by focusing on sectors like steel, machinery, and infrastructure.
 
• Under the plan, **heavy industries** such as steel plants in Bhilai, Durgapur, and Rourkela were established with assistance from countries like the Soviet Union, the UK, and Germany.
 
• The plan also aimed at achieving **economic self-sufficiency** and reducing dependence on foreign imports by strengthening industries that could produce capital goods and machinery.
 
• This strategic transition was driven by the vision of India becoming a **socialist economy**, with the state playing a dominant role in major industries, while agriculture was considered a secondary priority during this period.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **First Five-Year Plan (1951-1956):**

 
 
• The focus was primarily on **agriculture**, irrigation, and land reforms to address food shortages and support rural development.
 
• It emphasized **community development programs** and prioritized the agricultural sector to stabilize the newly independent economy.
 
• The plan achieved significant success in boosting **agricultural production** and laid the foundation for future economic planning.
 
 
 
• **Third Five-Year Plan (1961-1966):**
 
 
• The primary goal was to establish a **self-reliant economy** with an emphasis on agriculture and industry.
 
• However, this plan faced challenges due to the **Indo-China War (1962)**, the **Indo-Pak War (1965)**, and severe droughts, which diverted resources away from planned objectives.
 
• Despite setbacks, it contributed to the development of industries and infrastructure in India.
 
 
 
• **Fourth Five-Year Plan (1969-1974):**
 
 
• Focusing on **growth with stability** and reducing income inequality, this plan sought to address the disparities in economic development.
 
• It emphasized the **Green Revolution**, which transformed Indian agriculture through the introduction of high-yielding varieties of seeds, fertilizers, and irrigation infrastructure.
 
• The plan's success in agriculture helped India achieve food self-sufficiency.
 
 
 
• **Fifth Five-Year Plan (1974-1979):**
 
 
• This plan emphasized **poverty alleviation** and self-reliance, introducing programs like the **Minimum Needs Program** and the **Twenty-Point Program**.
 
• It also focused on achieving **economic growth** while addressing the basic needs of the population, such as food, housing, and healthcare.
 
 
 
• **Mahalnobis Model:**
 
 
• Introduced by **Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis**, this economic model formed the basis of the Second Five-Year Plan.
 
• The model emphasized the importance of **capital goods industries** to create a self-reliant economy and reduce dependence on foreign imports.
 
• It highlighted the role of the public sector in driving industrial growth and laid the foundation for India's mixed economy.

question:
Which of the following Five-Year Plans in India was notably criticized for its substantial dependence on foreign loans to finance the

import of machinery and capital goods?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Second Five-Year Plan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Second Five-Year Plan of India** (1956-1961) was heavily influenced by the **Soviet model of economic development**, emphasizing industrialization. This plan aimed to establish a strong foundation for industrial growth in the country.
 
• It placed significant importance on the development of **heavy industries**, such as iron and steel, heavy machinery, and coal mining. These sectors were considered essential for India's economic self-reliance.
 
• To finance the import of machinery, technology, and equipment required for these industries, the plan relied heavily on **foreign loans**. This dependence on external funding attracted criticism as it increased India's financial liabilities.
 
• The plan also focused on the establishment of public sector enterprises and the state’s role in managing economic activities. However, the reliance on foreign loans to fund industrial imports raised concerns about India’s economic sovereignty.
 
• Although the plan achieved considerable success in initiating industrial growth, its reliance on foreign financial support led to debates about the sustainability of such an approach. This issue became a key point of critique among economists and policymakers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Five-Year Plans in India:**

 
 
• The concept of Five-Year Plans was introduced in **1951** by the Indian government, inspired by the Soviet Union's planning model.
 
• These plans aimed to promote economic development by allocating resources to key sectors such as agriculture, industry, education, health, and infrastructure.
 
• The **Planning Commission** was responsible for formulating and implementing these plans until its dissolution in **2014**, when it was replaced by **NITI Aayog**.
 
 
 
• **Characteristics of the Second Five-Year Plan:**
 
 
• The Second Plan emphasized the establishment of basic industries, such as **steel plants, power generation, and machine building**.
 
• The plan was based on the **Mahalanobis model**, which prioritized industrialization over agriculture.
 
• It aimed to achieve a **4.5% annual growth rate**, focusing on long-term economic sustainability.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Five-Year Plans:**
 
 
• The **Fourth Five-Year Plan** (1969-1974) focused on growth with stability and self-reliance but did not rely heavily on foreign loans.
 
• The **Sixth Five-Year Plan** (1980-1985) prioritized poverty alleviation and employment generation through economic growth.
 
• The **Eighth Five-Year Plan** (1992-1997) emphasized private sector participation and liberalization of the economy.
 
 
 
• **Criticism of Foreign Loans:**
 
 
• While foreign loans provided essential resources for industrial development, they increased India’s **external debt burden**.
 
• Critics argued that reliance on foreign funding undermined economic independence and created vulnerabilities in times of global financial instability.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Mahalanobis Model:**

 
 
• Developed by **Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis**, this model focused on the rapid development of the industrial sector.
 
• It emphasized capital goods production as a driver of economic growth and prioritized heavy industry.
 
• This model influenced the planning strategy during the Second Five-Year Plan.
 
 
 
• **Public Sector Enterprises:**
 
 
• The Second Plan laid the foundation for the expansion of **public sector undertakings (PSUs)** in India.
 
• Key industries, such as steel plants at Bhilai, Rourkela, and Durgapur, were established during this period.
 
• The focus on PSUs aimed to reduce dependence on private enterprises and promote economic equality.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Indian Economy:**
 
 
• The Second Plan significantly contributed to the growth of the industrial sector and infrastructure development.
 
• However, the heavy reliance on foreign loans raised concerns about **debt repayment** and economic sovereignty.
 
• Despite its limitations, the plan played a crucial role in shaping India’s long-term economic strategies.

question: Which of the following is an indirect tax?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Excise Duty**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Indirect taxes** are those taxes where the incidence and impact of taxation fall on different entities. The tax is levied on **goods and services** rather than on the income, profit, or revenue of an individual or organization.
 
• **Excise Duty** is a form of indirect tax imposed on the **manufacture or production** of goods within the country. It is collected by the producer or manufacturer from the customer and then paid to the government.
 
• In the case of indirect taxes, the **tax burden** can be shifted from one person to another. For example, a manufacturer shifts the burden of excise duty to the retailer, who eventually shifts it to the **final consumer**.
 
• Since the implementation of the **Goods and Services Tax (GST)** on **July 1, 2017**, many indirect taxes, including **Central Excise Duty**, **Service Tax**, and **Value Added Tax (VAT)**, have been subsumed into a single taxation regime in India.
 
• However, excise duty is still applicable on certain items like **petroleum products** (petrol, diesel, aviation turbine fuel) and **tobacco products**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Direct Taxes:** These are taxes paid directly to the government by the person or organization on whom it is imposed. The burden cannot be shifted.

 
 
• **Income Tax:** Levied on the **annual income** of individuals, Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs), and other legal entities under the **Income Tax Act, 1961**.
 
• **Corporation Tax:** A direct tax imposed on the **net income or profit** that business enterprises or corporations make from their operations.
 
• **Wealth Tax:** A tax levied on the **market value of assets** (like jewelry, property, etc.) owned by an individual. In India, it was abolished in the **2015 Union Budget** and replaced with an additional **surcharge** on high-income earners.
 
 
 
• **Distinction:** While **Direct Taxes** are progressive (rate increases with income), **Indirect Taxes** are often considered regressive as they apply equally to all consumers regardless of their wealth or income levels.

question: ______ is land which is left fallow (uncultivated) for more than five years and can be brought under cultivation after improving it through reclamation practices.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Culturable wasteland**__.

__
 
• **Culturable Waste-Land:** Any land which is left fallow (uncultivated) for **more than five years** is included in this category.

 
 
• It can be brought under cultivation after improving it through reclamation practices.
 
 
 
• If the land is left uncultivated for **more than five years**, it would be categorized as culturable wasteland.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Permanent Pastures and Grazing Lands:** Most of this type of land is owned by the village** ‘Panchayat’ or the Government**. Only a small proportion of this land is **privately owned**.

 
 
• The land owned by the village panchayat comes under **‘Common Property Resources’**.
 
 
 
• **Current Fallow**:** **This is the land that is left without cultivation for one or less than one agricultural year.
 
 
• Fallowing is a cultural practice adopted for giving the land rest. The land** recoups lost fertility through natural processes**.

question:
In places, the groundwater is stored between layers of hard rock below the water table.

This is known as an _____.
solution:
The correct answer is __**aquifer.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **An aquifer** is an **underground layer of porous rocks or permeable rocks that store and retain groundwater levels in the soil.**
 
• The underground aquifer is built with all types of porous or permeable rock materials, such as **sand, gravel, or silt, making it a suitable water absorber.**
 
• The rainwater enters the aquifer through the** soil and becomes a part of the groundwater.**
 
• The groundwater from the aquifers then resurfaces from springs and wells.
 
• We can also extract the aquifer water with the help of a water well.
 
• The study of** groundwater, aquifer**, and their property is known as **hydrogeology.**

 [IMAGE: https://media.nationalgeographic.org/assets/photos/000/191/19125.jpg] 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Pond:**

 
 
• A **pond **is an area filled with water, either natural or artificial, that's lower than a lake.

The second layer of a forest, known as the understory, comprises small trees, shrubs, vines, and bushes.
 
• In a forest, the** middle layer **primarily consists of shrubs.
 
• **The bottom layer **of a forest, also known as the understory, is characterized by the presence of herbs and shrubs.

question: The natural vegetation of India is broadly divided into _______ groups.
solution:
The correct answer is __**5**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **India** boasts a rich and diverse array of natural vegetation, owing to its varied climatic conditions and geographical features.
 
• This natural vegetation can be broadly categorized into **five main types**:
 
• **Tropical Evergreen Forest: **These dense forests are characterized by lush greenery and high rainfall throughout the year. They are found in regions with warm and humid climates, such as the Western Ghats, northeastern states, and parts of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
 
• **Tropical Deciduous Forest:** Also known as monsoon forests, these forests experience distinct wet and dry seasons. They shed their leaves during the dry season to conserve water. Tropical deciduous forests are widespread in central and eastern India, including parts of the Deccan Plateau and the Eastern Ghats.
 
• **Thorny Bushes in Deserts:** Found in arid and semi-arid regions, such as the Thar Desert in Rajasthan, these vegetation types are adapted to survive in harsh desert conditions. They consist of drought-resistant plants like cacti and thorny shrubs.
 
• **Mountain Vegetation:** As altitude increases, vegetation varies based on temperature and precipitation. Mountain vegetation includes alpine meadows, coniferous forests, and temperate broadleaf forests. These vegetation types are found in the Himalayan region, including states like Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, and Jammu and Kashmir.
 
• **Mangrove Forest:** Mangroves thrive in coastal areas with brackish water and are characterized by salt-tolerant trees and shrubs. They provide important habitats for various marine species and act as natural barriers against coastal erosion. Mangrove forests are found along the coastlines of states like West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, and Tamil Nadu.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• India's natural vegetation is shaped by factors such as **soil composition, climate, topography, and precipitation **patterns.
 
• This diverse range of flora and fauna contributes to India's rich biodiversity and ecological significance.

__
 
• **Khadar** refers to the** fresh alluvial sediment** deposited by periodic floods in the **Ganga Plain**.
 
• Also known as **"new alluvial soil," **Khadar is typically located in the floodplains of rivers such as the Ganges.
 
• It primarily consists of fine silts that are annually deposited by** floodwaters, **contributing to soil enrichment.
 
• Characterized by its fertility, Khadar soil benefits from the regular deposition of nutrient-rich sediments during flood events.
 
• It often exhibits a higher concentration of salts, derived from the river's water, which is replenished with each flooding cycle.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **The Ganga Plain**, also referred to as the Indo-Gangetic Plain, spans approximately 700,000 square kilometers across the Indian subcontinent.
 
• Encompassing regions of northern and eastern India, eastern Pakistan, Bangladesh, and the southern plains of Nepal, it stands as a fertile expanse.
 
• This vast floodplain is shaped by the convergence of major rivers, including the Indus, Brahmaputra, and Ganga, which traverse its expanse.
 
• Situated within the foreland basin of the Himalayas, the plain's landscape remains largely flat, characterized by soil deposits rather than mountainous terrain.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Bhangar **represents an older type of **alluvial soil, **characterized by its lesser fertility and sandy composition. Composed of aged alluvium, Bhangar soil tends to exhibit a darker hue.

question: ________ land is suitable for cropping on a regular basis.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Arable**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Arable land, **derived from the** Latin word "arābilis," **refers to **land that is suitable for regular cropping due to its ploughable nature and fertile soil.**
 
• This category encompasses** land utilized for temporary crops, temporary meadows, kitchen gardens, and market gardens.**
 
• Additionally, it includes land that remains temporarily fallow for periods of less than five years.
 
• Arable land is typically cultivated under a system of crop rotation, benefiting from nutrient-dense soils, ample sunlight, and predictable temperatures. However, despite its potential, arable land has finite capacity for agricultural production.
 
• The ability to cultivate crops is influenced by various factors including climate, soil quality, and management practices.
 
• For instance, farmers may opt to let a piece of land "lie fallow" to replenish depleted soil fertility. This practice helps optimize agricultural productivity by maintaining soil health and maximizing crop yields over time.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Urban land **refers to the territory encompassed within the boundaries of an urban area, excluding agricultural zones. This type of land is primarily dedicated to residential, commercial, industrial, and institutional purposes, serving the needs of urban populations.
 
• **Barren land**, on the other hand, describes areas characterized by poor soil quality, minimal biodiversity, or sparse vegetation. Such land typically lacks the necessary conditions to support robust plant growth or sustain diverse ecosystems.
 
• **Marginal land**, also known as pasture land or grassland, refers to areas with limited agricultural or industrial value.

subject: GK
question:
The "Indian Forest Act" of 1878 categorized forests into reserved and protected areas.

What was a key difference in the treatment and rights of local communities between these two categories?

options.text: Both categories granted complete autonomy to local communities in forest management.
In reserved forests, all traditional rights of local communities were extinguished, while some limited rights were permitted in protected forests.
Protected forests were exclusively for commercial exploitation by the British, while reserved forests were for local use.
There was no significant difference in the restrictions imposed on local communities between the two categories.

solution:
The correct answer is __**In reserved forests, all traditional rights of local communities were extinguished, while some limited rights were permitted in protected forests.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Indian Forest Act of 1878** was a colonial legislative measure designed to consolidate **British** control over **India's forest resources**, classifying them into **Reserved**, **Protected**, and **Village forests**.
 
• **Reserved Forests** were the most restricted category; the government claimed full ownership of these areas, which contained the most valuable timber like **Teak** and **Sal**. In these zones, all **customary rights** of local communities, including **grazing**, **collection of minor forest produce**, and **entry**, were **legally extinguished** unless specific permission was granted.
 
• In contrast, **Protected Forests** allowed for some **limited rights**. While the government still owned the land, local communities could often access these areas for **firewood** or **grazing**, provided they did not damage the species protected for commercial use. The legal logic was that everything was **permitted unless specifically prohibited**.
 
• This classification system effectively turned forest dwellers into **encroachers** on their own ancestral lands, prioritizing the **commercial extraction** of timber for **railway sleepers** and **shipbuilding** over the subsistence needs of **indigenous populations**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dietrich Brandis**:

 
 
• A **German botanist** who became the first **Inspector General of Forests** in India and helped found the **Imperial Forest School** at **Dehradun** in **1878**.
 
• He introduced **Scientific Forestry**, which replaced natural biodiversity with **plantations** of specific industrial species to ensure a steady supply of timber.
 
 
 
• **Village Forests**:
 
 
• The third category established by the **1878 Act**, where portions of **reserved forests** could be assigned to village communities for their direct use, though this provision was rarely utilized by the administration.
 
 
 
• **Social Consequences**:
 
 
• The restrictions led to widespread **hardship** and **displacement** for **Adivasi** communities, triggering major historical uprisings like the **Bastar Rebellion** of **1910** and movements led by **Birsa Munda**.

question: Which Union Territory recorded the highest male literacy rate, according to the 2011 Census?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Lakshadweep**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Lakshadweep** boasts the highest literacy rate among **Union Territories, standing at 92.28%**.
 
• Bihar holds the lowest literacy rate in India, with 63.82%. Male literacy achieves its peak in Lakshadweep at 96.11%, closely followed by Kerala at 96.02%.
 
• Kerala also leads in female literacy with 91.98%, while Mizoram follows closely with 89.40%.
 
• Bihar records the lowest male literacy rate at 73.39%, while Rajasthan holds the lowest female literacy rate at 52.66%.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

__
 
• **The 2011 census of India**, also known as the **15th Indian census, **was carried out in two phases:** house listing and population enumeration.**
 
• Commencing on April 1, 2010, the house listing phase involved gathering data on all buildings. Additionally, information for the National Population Register (NPR) was collected during this phase, intending to assign a 12-digit unique identification number to all registered Indian residents by the Unique Identification Authority of India.
 
• The second phase, population enumeration, occurred between February 9 and 28, 2011. Notably, the 2011 census marked the first instance of collecting biometric information.
 
• Census-taking in India dates back to 1872. As per the provisional reports released on March 31, 2011, the Indian population surged to 1.21 billion, exhibiting a decadal growth rate of 17.70%.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lakshadweep**, a union territory of India, comprises an archipelago of 36 islands divided into three island subgroups. These include the Laccadive Islands situated in the middle, the Amindivi Islands in the north, and the atoll of Minicoy in the south.
 
• They are geographically demarcated by the 11th parallel north separating the Laccadive and Amindivi Islands, and the Nine Degree Channel along the 9th parallel north separating Minicoy.
 
• Positioned between the Arabian Sea to the west and the Laccadive Sea to the east, these islands are situated approximately 220–440 km (140–270 mi) off the Malabar Coast of mainland India.
 
• The collective land area of the islands is approximately 32.62 km², with a population of 64,473 as per the 2011 census across the 10 inhabited islands.

question: The ________ birth rate indicates the number of live births occurring during the year per 1000 population estimated at midyear.
solution:
The correct answer is __**crude**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The crude birth rate **indicates the** number of live births **occurring during the year **per 1000 population** estimated at midyear.
 
• The crude birth rate (CBR) represents the number of live births per 1,000 individuals in a population within a specific year.
 
• It's calculated by dividing the total number of live births during the year by the mid-year population and then multiplying by 1,000.
 
• This statistic, which is not adjusted for seasonal variations, serves as a key demographic and socioeconomic indicator.
 
• The CBR is instrumental in determining the** rate of natural population growth, excluding migration.**
 
• It's derived as a ratio, where the numerator is the number of live births within a defined time frame, and the denominator is the total person-years lived by the population during that period.
 
• Data on CBR is sourced from various channels, including birth and death registration systems, censuses, sample surveys conducted by **national statistical agencies **and other organizations, and demographic analysis.
 
• For example, in 2021, the United States recorded a CBR of 11.0 births per 1,000 people.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Crude birth rate: Number of live births per 1,000 population: (Number of live births / Estimated midyear Population) x 1,000 **

question: Which of the following best defines population density in the context of India's demographic studies?

options.text: The number of people living in urban areas of a state
The ratio of employed individuals to the total population
The number of persons per unit area of land
The total population of a country divided by its total income

solution:
The correct answer is __**The number of persons per unit area of land**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Population density** is defined as the number of persons living per unit area of land, usually expressed as persons per square kilometer.
 
• It is a critical demographic indicator that helps understand the spatial distribution of population across a region or country.
 
• In the context of India, the average population density according to the **2011 Census** was 382 persons per square kilometer.
 
• High population density is observed in states like **Bihar, West Bengal, and Kerala**, while states like Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram have low population density.
 
• Population density is influenced by factors such as **geography, climate, availability of resources, and urbanization**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: The number of people living in urban areas of a state**

 
 
• This refers to the urban population of a state or region, not the overall population density.
 
• Urban areas tend to have a higher population density due to concentrated infrastructure, industries, and employment opportunities.
 
• In India, as per the **2011 Census**, approximately 31% of the total population resided in urban areas.
 
 
 
• **Option 2: The ratio of employed individuals to the total population**
 
 
• This defines the **employment-to-population ratio**, which is an economic indicator showing the proportion of a country's working-age population that is employed.
 
• It is not related to population density but is used to analyze labor market conditions.
 
• As per the **Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) 2021-22**, India's employment-to-population ratio for individuals aged 15 years and above was approximately 39.8%.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: The total population of a country divided by its total income**
 
 
• This concept is unrelated to population density and refers to economic measures like per capita income or GDP per capita.
 
• Per capita income provides an estimate of the average income earned per person in a given area in a specific time period.
 
• It is calculated by dividing the total income of a region by its total population.
 
 
 
• **Population Density: A Key Demographic Measure**
 
 
• Population density provides insights into resource allocation, urban planning, and infrastructure development.
 
• Regions with high population density often face challenges like overcrowding, resource scarcity, and environmental degradation.
 
• On the other hand, regions with low population density may struggle with underutilized resources and lack of economic opportunities.

question: Which of the following statements correctly defines population stabilization?

options.text: It refers to the stage where fertility becomes higher than mortality
It refers to zero birth rate
It occurs when the difference between birth rate and death rate is negligible
It indicates exponential growth of urban population

solution:
The correct answer is __**It occurs when the difference between birth rate and death rate is negligible**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Population stabilization refers to the stage where the total population of a region or country stabilizes due to a negligible difference between birth rate and death rate.
 
• This occurs when the fertility rate declines to the replacement level fertility, which is approximately 2.1 children per woman.
 
• It is an essential demographic milestone that signifies a balanced population growth and plays a crucial role in sustainable development.
 
• Population stabilization leads to reduced pressure on resources such as food, water, healthcare, and infrastructure.
 
• India has been actively working towards achieving population stabilization through initiatives like the National Population Policy (2000) and programs promoting family planning and reproductive health.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: It refers to the stage where fertility becomes higher than mortality**
 
 
• This statement is incorrect as higher fertility compared to mortality leads to population growth, not stabilization.
 
• Population growth occurs when the birth rate significantly exceeds the death rate, which is common in developing countries.
 
 
 
• **Option 2: It refers to zero birth rate**
 
 
• Zero birth rate implies no births are taking place, which is not population stabilization but a scenario of population decline.
 
• Population stabilization focuses on maintaining a balance, not eliminating births altogether.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: It indicates exponential growth of urban population**
 
 
• Exponential urban population growth refers to rapid migration and population increase in urban areas, leading to urbanization.
 
• This phenomenon is unrelated to population stabilization, which concerns the overall population equilibrium.
 
 
 
• **Population Stabilization: Key Terminologies**
 
 
• **Replacement Level Fertility:** The level of fertility at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next, typically 2.1 children per woman.
 
• **Birth Rate:** The number of live births per 1,000 people in a year.
 
• **Death Rate:** The number of deaths per 1,000 people in a year.
 
• **Demographic Transition:** The process by which a country moves from high birth and death rates to low birth and death rates, achieving population stabilization.

subject: GK
question:
Consider the following statements about India's population growth since 1981 and choose the correct option:

1. The rate of population growth began to decline gradually after 1981.

2. Birth rates continued to rise sharply in the 1990s.

3. Despite declining growth rate, 182 million people were added in the 1990s.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 1 and 3 are correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement 1: The rate of population growth began to decline gradually after 1981** - This statement is **correct**. After 1981, India experienced a gradual decline in the population growth rate due to increased awareness about family planning, implementation of government policies, and socio-economic changes.
 
• **Statement 2: Birth rates continued to rise sharply in the 1990s**. This statement is **incorrect**. During the 1990s, birth rates in India began to decline as a result of better healthcare, education, and family planning measures.
 
• **Statement 3: Despite the declining growth rate, 182 million people were added in the 1990s**. This statement is **correct**. Even though the growth rate was declining, the population base was already large, leading to the addition of 182 million people in the 1990s.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Population Growth in India:**

 
 
• India's population growth peaked during the 1960s and 1970s, primarily due to high birth rates and declining death rates as a result of improvements in healthcare and sanitation.
 
• Since 1981, the growth rate has been declining due to better family planning and awareness initiatives.
 
 
 
• **Factors Contributing to Declining Growth Rates:**
 
 
• Increased literacy rates, especially among women.
 
• Government initiatives like the National Population Policy (2000) aimed at stabilizing the population.
 
• Access to contraceptives and better healthcare services.
 
 
 
• **Challenges Despite Decline:**
 
 
• India's population remains one of the largest in the world, contributing to challenges like urban overcrowding, unemployment, and resource depletion.
 
• The demographic dividend of a young population requires sustainable policies in education, skill development, and employment.
 
 
 
• **Key Population Statistics:**
 
 
• India added approximately 181 million people between 1991 and 2001, despite a declining growth rate.
 
• The total fertility rate (TFR) in India has been steadily decreasing. As of the latest estimates, it is nearing the replacement level of 2.1.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **National Population Policy (2000):**

 
 
• Aimed at achieving population stabilization by 2045.
 
• Key goals include reducing the infant mortality rate to below 30 per 1,000 live births and achieving universal access to contraception.
 
 
 
• **Demographic Transition in India:**
 
 
• India is currently in the third stage of demographic transition, characterized by declining birth and death rates.
 
• With continuous efforts, India is expected to achieve replacement-level fertility soon.
 
 
 
• **Global Perspective:**
 
 
• India is expected to surpass China as the most populous country by the late 2020s, according to United Nations projections.
 
• Despite the challenges, India’s demographic dividend offers significant potential for economic growth if harnessed effectively.

question: Which of the following states or UTs had the smallest population in 2011?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Lakshadweep**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• According to the **2011 Census of India**, **Lakshadweep** had the smallest population among all states and Union Territories in India.
 
• The total population of Lakshadweep was **64,473**, making it the least populated Union Territory.
 
• **Sikkim**, while being the least populated state, had a population of **610,577**, which is significantly higher than Lakshadweep.
 
• Other states such as **Mizoram** (population: 1,091,014) and **Arunachal Pradesh** (population: 1,382,611) also had larger populations compared to Lakshadweep.
 
• Lakshadweep is a group of **36 small islands** and is geographically the smallest Union Territory in India, contributing to its low population density.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Lakshadweep:**

 
 
• It is located in the **Arabian Sea**, off the southwestern coast of India.
 
• It consists of **36 islands**, including **10 inhabited islands**, **17 uninhabited islands**, and others comprising lagoons and reefs.
 
• The official language is **Malayalam**, and the primary occupation of the residents is fishing and coconut farming.
 
• It has a **high literacy rate** of approximately **91.85%** as per the 2011 Census.
 
• Lakshadweep is known for its **pristine beaches**, coral reefs, and marine biodiversity.
 
 
 
• **Sikkim:**
 
 
• Sikkim is located in the northeastern part of India and is bordered by Bhutan, Nepal, and China.
 
• It is the **least populated state in India**, with a population of **610,577** as per the 2011 Census.
 
• Sikkim is known for its **natural beauty**, including the **Himalayan mountain ranges** and biodiversity.
 
• The state capital is **Gangtok**, and the official languages include Nepali, Lepcha, and Bhutia.
 
• Sikkim has achieved recognition for its environmental initiatives, such as being the first fully **organic state** in India.
 
 
 
• **Mizoram:**
 
 
• Mizoram is located in the northeastern region of India and is bordered by Myanmar and Bangladesh.
 
• It had a population of **1,091,014** according to the 2011 Census.
 
• The primary language spoken is **Mizo**, and agriculture is the main occupation of its residents.
 
• Mizoram is known for its **lush landscapes** and bamboo forests.
 
• The state capital is **Aizawl**.
 
 
 
• **Arunachal Pradesh:**
 
 
• Arunachal Pradesh is the northeasternmost state of India, sharing borders with Bhutan, Myanmar, and China.
 
• It had a population of **1,382,611** as per the 2011 Census.
 
• The state is renowned for its **tribal diversity**, with over **26 major tribes** and numerous sub-tribes.
 
• The official language is **English**, and the state capital is **Itanagar**.
 
• Arunachal Pradesh is rich in natural resources, including forests, rivers, and mountains.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Population Density:**

 
 
• Lakshadweep has the **lowest population** due to its small geographical size and limited inhabitable area.
 
• Among states, **Sikkim** ranks the lowest in terms of population.
 
• The population density of Lakshadweep is higher compared to some northeastern states due to its smaller land area.
 
 
 
• **2011 Census:**
 
 
• The 2011 Census provided crucial data about population distribution, density, and demographics across India.
 
• It highlighted the **diverse population** characteristics of India's states and Union Territories.

subject: GK
question: What do the words ‘aus’, ‘aman’ and ‘boro’ signify in the context of agricultural calendar in India?

options.text: Types of seasons of sowing rice in West Bengal
Types of traditional wells in Gujarat
Types of alluvial soils in the Gangetic plains
Types of harvest festivals in Assam

solution:
The correct answer is __**Types of seasons of sowing rice in West Bengal.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the context of the agricultural calendar in India, ‘aus’, ‘aman’, and ‘boro’ refer to three **distinct varieties of rice crops** that are grown in different seasons, particularly in the** eastern regions like West Bengal, Bihar, and Bangladesh.**
 
• **Aus**:
 
 
• **Season**: Sown in March-April and harvested in July-August.
 
• **Characteristics**: Aus rice is typically a **rain-fed crop** and is grown during the early monsoon period. It matures quickly and is often grown on upland areas.
 
 
 
• **Aman**:
 
 
• **Season**: Sown in June-July and harvested in November-December.
 
• **Characteristics**: Aman rice is grown in the main monsoon season and is **heavily dependent on the rains.** It is the most important rice crop in regions like West Bengal.
 
 
 
• **Boro**:
 
 
• **Season**: Sown in December-January and harvested in April-May.
 
• **Characteristics**: Boro rice is cultivated during the dry winter season with irrigation. It requires** controlled water supply **and is grown in low-lying areas.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Types of Traditional Wells in Gujarat

 
 
• **Vav/Stepwells:** These are intricately designed wells with steps leading down to the water. Famous for their architectural beauty, such as the Rani ki Vav in Patan.
 
• **Kua**: Traditional open wells used for drawing water manually, common in rural areas, and typically built near farms for irrigation.
 
 
 
• Types of Alluvial Soils in the Gangetic Plains
 
 
• **Khadar**: The newer, fertile alluvial soil deposited by rivers, found near riverbanks and floodplains. It is renewed annually during floods and is highly suitable for agriculture.
 
• **Bhangar**: The older alluvial soil found at higher elevations, slightly less fertile than Khadar due to the presence of calcium carbonate nodules (kankar).
 
 
 
• Types of Harvest Festivals in Assam
 
 
• **Bihu (Rongali Bihu)**: The most popular harvest festival, celebrated in April to mark the Assamese New Year and the start of the sowing season.

• Gandak:

 
 
• Gandak River, also called the Narayani River, river in central Nepal and northern India.
 
• It is formed by the union of the Kali and Trisuli rivers, which rise in the Great Himalaya Range in Nepal; from this junction to the Indian border the river is called the Narayani.
 
• It flows southwest into India and then turns southeast along with the Uttar Pradesh–Bihar state border and across the Indo-Gangetic Plain.
 
• It enters the Ganges (Ganga) River opposite Patna after a winding course of 475 miles (765 km).
 
• The Burhi (“Old”) Gandak flows parallel to and east of the Gandak River in an old channel.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• The Chambal is the chief tributary of the Yamuna River and rises in the Vindhya Range just south of Mhow, western Madhya Pradesh state.
 
• From its source, it flows north into the southeastern Rajasthan state. 
 
• Turning northeast, it flows past Kota and along the Rajasthan–Madhya Pradesh border; shifting east-southeast, it forms a portion of the **Uttar Pradesh-Madhya Pradesh border** and flows through Uttar Pradesh to empty into the Yamuna after a 550-mile (900-km) course.
 
• The Banas, Kali Sindh, Sipra, and Parbati are its chief tributaries.
 
 
 
• **Godavari is the largest peninsular river in India.**

• Major right bank tributaries: Pravara, Manjira, and Manair rivers.
 
• The Pranhita river is the largest tributary of Godavari.
 
• Important dams built across the Godavari river: Jayakwadi dam, Gangapur Dam, Babli project, and Sriram Sagar Dam.
 
• The Coringa mangrove forest is situated in the Godavari delta.
 
 
 
• Narmada River 
 
 
• Is the longest river of Madhya Pradesh, followed by the Tapti. 
 
• The Source of the Narmada is Narmada Kund which is located at Amarkantak in Anuppur District, Madhya Pradesh.
 
• The Narmada is also known as the Rewa.
 
• People from Madhya Pradesh depend fully on the Narmada River, they consider Narmada as the Life Line of Madhya Pradesh.
 
• It is one of the major rivers in India that run from east to west along with the Tapti and the Mahi.
 
• It flows through the states of Madhya Pradesh (1,077 km), Maharashtra (74 km), and in Gujarat (161 km).

• **The agreement establishes a 30-year water-sharing arrangement that divides the Ganges waters between India and Bangladesh based on the time of year and the flow of the river. **
 
• The agreement also includes provisions for the construction of joint projects to augment the flow of the Ganges and improve water management in the region.
 
• The Farakka Agreement has been hailed as a success story in international water diplomacy.
 
• It has helped to improve relations between India and Bangladesh and has provided a framework for the sustainable management of shared water resources.

• **Nepal:-**

• It is a landlocked country, with no direct access to the sea.

subject: GK
question: The drainage system formed when rivers discharge their waters from all directions in a lake or depression, as in the case of Loktak Lake in Manipur, is called ________.
solution:
The Correct Answer is **centripetal.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__****Centripetal Drainage Pattern:**

__
 
• It is just the opposite of the radial as streams flow toward a central depression.
 
• During wetter portions of the year, these streams feed ephemeral lakes, which evaporate away during dry periods.
 
• Sometimes, salt flats are also created in these dry lake beds as salt dissolved in the lake water precipitates out of solution and is left behind when the water evaporates away.
 
• **E.g. Loktak lake in Manipur.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

**Radial Drainage Pattern:**

 
• The radial drainage pattern develops around a central elevated point and is common to conically shaped features such as volcanoes.
 
• When the rivers originate from a hill and flow in all directions, the drainage pattern is known as ‘radial’.
 
• E.g. The rivers originating from the** Amarkantak range; Narmada** and **Son (tributary of Ganga).**

**Trellis Drainage Pattern:**

 
• Trellis drainage develops in folded topography where hard and soft rocks exist parallel to each other.
 
• Down-turned folds called synclines form valleys in which reside the main channel of the stream.
 
• Such a pattern is formed when the primary tributaries of main rivers flow parallel to each other and secondary tributaries join them at right angles.
 
• **E.g. The rivers in the upper part of the Himalayan region; Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra.**

**Dendritic Drainage Pattern:**

 
• It is the most common form and resembles the branching pattern of tree roots.
 
• The dendritic pattern develops where the river channel follows the slope of the terrain.
 
• The pattern develops in areas where the rock beneath the stream has no particular structure and can be eroded equally easily in all directions.
 
• Tributaries join larger streams at acute angles (less than 90°).
 
• **E.g. The rivers of the northern plains; Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/733ba9d541c73d179444da7d84d38741a60e28b6751039dc140626fe14c3488f.png]

question: ________ are NOT considered surface water.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Aquifers**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Aquifers** are **underground layers** of **water-bearing rock**.
 
• They are **not considered surface water** because they are **beneath the Earth's surface**.
 
• **Surface water** refers to **bodies of water above the ground**, such as oceans, lakes, and rivers.
 
• **Aquifers** are a **crucial source of groundwater** but are **distinct** from **surface water**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Oceans**

 
 
• **Oceans** are **large bodies of saltwater** that cover the majority of the **Earth's surface**.
 
• They are considered **surface water** because they are** located** on the **Earth's exterior**.
 
• Oceans play a critical role in regulating the **planet's climate**, **weather patterns**, and **ecosystems**.
 
 
 
• **Lakes**
 
 
• **Lakes** are** large bodies** of** water** that are **surrounded by land**.
 
• They are considered **surface water **because they exist a**bove the Earth's surface**.
 
• Lakes can vary **greatly in size**, **depth,** and **characteristics**.
 
 
 
• **Rivers**
 
 
• **Rivers** are **natural watercourses **that flow from **higher to lower** **elevations**, usually towards the sea or another body of water.
 
• They are classified as **surface water** as they flow **above the Earth's surface**.
 
• Rivers play a crucial role in the **hydrological cycle**, **transporting water**, **sediment**, and **nutrients across landscapes**.

__
 
• Brahmaputra River

 
 
• ​The Brahmaputra, one of the largest rivers in the world, has its origin in the Chemayungdung glacier of the Kailash range near the Mansarovar lake.

 
 
• From here, it traverses eastward longitudinally for a distance of nearly 1,200 km in a dry and flat region of southern Tibet, where it is known as the Tsangpo, which means 'the purifier'.
 
• The Rango Tsangpo is the major right-bank tributary of this river in Tibet. It emerges as a turbulent and dynamic river after carving out a deep gorge in the Central Himalayas near Namcha Barwa (7,755 m).
 
• The river emerges from the foothills under the name of Siang or Dihang.
 
 
 
• It enters India from Arunachal Pradesh.
 
 
• Flowing southwest, it receives its main left-bank tributaries, viz., Dibang or Sikang and Lohit, thereafter, it is known as the Brahmaputra.
 
 
 
• The Brahmaputra receives numerous tributaries in its 750 km long journey through the Assam valley.
 
 
• Its major left bank tributaries are the Burhi Dihing and Dhansari (South) whereas the important right bank tributaries are the Subansiri, Kameng, Manas and Sankosh. The Subansiri which has its origin in Tibet, is an antecedent river.
 
 
 
• The Brahmaputra enters Bangladesh near Dhubri and flows southward.
 
 
• In Bangladesh, the Tista joins it on its right bank from where the river is known as the Jamuna.
 
• It finally merges with the river Padma, which falls in the Bay of Bengal.

• It flows through the states of Maharashtra, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh.
 
• Tributaries:
 
 
• Left bank: Banganga, Kadva, Shivana, Purna, Kadam, Pranahita, Indravati, Taliperu, Sabari, Dharna.
 
• Right bank: Nasardi, Pravara, Sindphana, Manjira, Manair, Kinnerasani.
 
 
 
 
 
• **Ganga****​**
 
 
• The Ganga rises from the Gangotri glacier near Gomukh in the Uttarkashi district of the state of Uttarakhand.
 
• The total length of the Ganga is about 2,525 km.
 
• The river is bounded by the Himalayas on the north, by the Aravalli on the west, by the Vindhyas and Chhotanagpur plateau on the south, and by the Brahmaputra Ridge on the east.
 
• Left Tributaries: Karnali, Mahakali, Gandak, Kosi Ramganga, Ghagra,Mahananda etc.
 
• Right Tributaries: Yamuna, Son, Damodar, Ken.
 
 
 
• **Krishna**
 
 
• **​**Krishna is the **second largest peninsular river** flowing towards the east.
 
• It originates near **Mahabaleshwar** from the Sahyadri mountain range.
 
• The delta formed by Krishna is an example of a **bird's foot delta(Mississippi type)**
 
• The major tributaries of the Krishna are Koyana, Ghatprabha, Malaprabha, Tungabhadra, Musi, and Bhima.

question:
Choose the correct statement about the peninsular rivers.

a. The Narmada rises in the Malwa plateau.

b. The Godavari rises from the slopes of the Western Ghats near Nashik.

c. The Mahanadi rises in the highlands of Chhattisgarh.

d. The Krishna rises from a spring near Mahabaleshwar.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only b, c and d**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Only b, c, and d** are correct statements about the peninsular rivers of India.
 
• The Godavari rises from the slopes of the Western Ghats near Nashik.
 
• The Mahanadi rises in the highlands of Chhattisgarh.
 
• The Krishna rises from a spring near Mahabaleshwar.
 
• The Narmada, however, does not rise in the Malwa plateau; it rises in the Amarkantak plateau.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The peninsular rivers of India are primarily rain-fed and have a seasonal flow pattern.
 
• These rivers flow through the Deccan Plateau and are characterized by their mature stage, having wider valleys and lower gradients.
 
• Major peninsular rivers include the Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, and Mahanadi, which flow eastwards into the Bay of Bengal.
 
• The Narmada and Tapti are notable exceptions as they flow westwards into the Arabian Sea.

__
 
• Tawa Reservoir is a reservoir on the **Tawa River in central India**. **It is located in Itarsi of Hoshangabad District of Madhya Pradesh state**, above Betul district.
 
• The reservoir was formed by the construction of the Tawa Dam, which began in 1958 and was** completed in 1978.**
 
• The dam** provides water for irrigation in Hoshangabad and Harda districts**.
 
• The Tawa reservoir forms the **western boundary of Satpura National Park and Bori Wildlife Sanctuary.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The **Tawa Matsya Sangh** – a federation of Fisherworker’s cooperatives – an organization fighting for the rights of the displaced forest dwellers of the Satpura forest in Madhya Pradesh.
 
• The newly formed Tawa Matsya Sangh (TMS) organized rallies and a chakka jam (road blockade), demanding their right to continue fishing for their livelihood.
 
• In response to their protests, the government created a committee to assess the issue.
 
• The committee recommended that fishing rights be granted to the villagers for their livelihood.
 
• **In 1996, the Madhya Pradesh government decided to give to the people displaced by the Tawa dam the fishing rights for the reservoir.**
