solution:
The Correct Answer is __**Firoz Shah Tuglaq**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• **Firoz Shah Tughlaq(1351-89)**

 
 
• After the death of Muhammad-bin**-Tughlaq** in 1351, he was chosen as sultan by the nobles.
 
• He strictly followed the advice of the ulemas in running the administration. 
 
• He pleased the nobles and assured hereditary succession to their properties. 
 
• Thus the iqta system was not only revived but also it was made hereditary.
 
• Four new taxes were introduced- 
 
 
• Kharaj - the land tax= 1/10 of the produce.
 
• Zakat - 2.5% tax on property.
 
• Jizya - protection tax paid by permanent non-muslims residents to rulers.
 
• Khams - 1/5th tax on Mines, treasure troves, and a share on war booty
 
 
 
• He was the first Sultan to impose an irrigation tax. 
 
• But at the same time, he dug irrigation canals and wells. 
 
• The longest canal was about 200 kilometres from Sutlej to Hansi. 
 
• Another canal was between Yamuna and Hissar.
 
• Diwani-i-Khairat -A department to make provisions for the marriage of poor girls was established.
 
• Dur-ul-Shifa - A hospital in Delhi was established.
 
• He started the imposition of Jizya on Brahmans.
 
• He imposed water cess Haq-i-shrib.

question: The Chahalgani (Group of Forty) nobles were formed during the reign of:
solution:
The correct answer is __**Iltutmish**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• **Iltutmish** (reigned **1211−1236 AD**), the third ruler of the **Mamluk Dynasty**, is credited with the creation of the **Turkan-i-Chahalgani**, also known as the **Corps of Forty**.

• The **Chahalgani** was an elite body of forty loyal **Turkish slave officers** who were handpicked by the Sultan to manage the administration and military affairs of the **Delhi Sultanate**.

• The formation of this group was a strategic move by **Iltutmish** to counter the influence of senior **Ghurid nobles** and to consolidate his power after the death of **Qutb-ud-din Aibak**.

• These nobles held significant positions such as **Iqtadars** (land-grant holders) and played a crucial role in maintaining the stability of the empire against internal rebellions and **Mongol** threats.

• The group functioned as the executive council of the Sultan, although they eventually became so powerful that they started interfering in the **succession** of the throne after **Iltutmish** died.

 **Additional Information__**

• **Balban**:

• He was originally a member of the **Chahalgani** but later became the Sultan of Delhi.

• Recognizing that the group posed a threat to the **absolute monarchy**, he systematically eliminated its members to restore the prestige of the crown.

• He is famous for his policy of **Blood and Iron** and the introduction of **Sijda** and **Paibos** (prostration and kissing the Sultan's feet).

• **Qutb-ud-din Aibak**:

• He was the founder of the **Slave Dynasty** in **1206 AD** and the builder of the **Quwwat-ul-Islam** mosque.

• He was known as **Lakh Baksh** due to his extreme generosity toward his subjects.

• **Alauddin Khalji**:

• A prominent ruler of the **Khalji Dynasty** known for his extensive **agrarian and market reforms**.

• He introduced the **Dagh** (branding of horses) and **Chehra** (descriptive rolls for soldiers) to prevent corruption in the military.

__
 
• The **Chola inscription at Uttaramerur** primarily deals with the system of **village administration**. It provides detailed insights into how the villages under the Chola dynasty were governed.
 
• The inscription, dated back to the **10th century CE**, highlights a highly organized and democratic form of governance at the village level.
 
• It describes the functioning of **local assemblies** (sabhas) and the process of electing members to these assemblies through a **lottery system**.
 
• The inscription emphasizes the qualifications required for candidates to be part of the village administration, such as **land ownership, moral integrity, and educational qualifications**.
 
• It also outlines the responsibilities and powers of these assemblies, including decisions regarding **tax collection, dispute resolution, and maintenance of public infrastructure**.
 
• This historical document showcases the advanced administrative capabilities of the **Chola Empire** and its emphasis on decentralized governance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• The Chola dynasty was one of the longest-ruling dynasties in Indian history, flourishing between the **9th and 13th centuries CE**.
 
• It was known for its contributions to **art, architecture, and administration**.
 
• The Cholas established a highly efficient administrative system with a strong emphasis on **local self-governance**.
 
 
 
• **Uttaramerur Inscription:**
 
 
• The Uttaramerur inscription is one of the most detailed records of village administration in ancient India.
 
• It was discovered in the temple town of **Uttaramerur** in modern-day Tamil Nadu.
 
• The inscription provides evidence of a highly democratic system where even common villagers had a say in the administration.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of Village Administration:**
 
 
• Village assemblies were called **Sabhas**, and they were responsible for governing the village.
 
• Members of the sabha were chosen through a **lottery system** to ensure fairness and avoid nepotism.
 
• Sub-committees handled various aspects of governance, such as **finance, justice, and public works**.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Aspects:**
 
 
• The inscription does not focus on topics like **maritime trade**, **military conquests**, or **temple rituals**, which were other significant aspects of Chola governance but are not the subject of this document.
 
• Instead, it serves as a testament to the importance of **decentralized governance** and the empowerment of local communities in the Chola Empire.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Significance of the Chola Administration:**

 
 
• The Chola system of governance is often seen as a precursor to modern democratic principles, as it allowed for **elected representation** and public participation.
 
• The administrative practices documented in the Uttaramerur inscription reflect a high level of **political sophistication**.
 
• This system ensured transparency and accountability, which were crucial for the effective functioning of the empire.
 
 
 
• **Global Recognition:**
 
 
• The Chola administrative system is studied worldwide for its **innovative governance** models.
 
• It provides valuable lessons in **decentralization and participatory governance**.

subject: GK
question: Neither the Iqta system nor the Mansabdari system was prevalent under the:
solution:
The correct answer is __**Vijayanagara Empire**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Iqta system** was a prominent administrative system established during the **Delhi Sultanate**. It involved the allocation of land (Iqta) to nobles and officers in return for administrative and military services. This system was not present in the **Vijayanagara Empire**.
 
• The **Mansabdari system**, introduced by the Mughal Emperor Akbar, was a military-administrative system where officers (Mansabdars) were ranked based on their military responsibilities and assigned jagirs (land revenue assignments). This system was not a part of the **Vijayanagara Empire**.
 
• The **Vijayanagara Empire** (1336-1646) followed a feudal administrative structure, where land was governed by local chieftains, known as Nayakas, under the Nayankara system. This system was distinct from both the Iqta and Mansabdari systems.
 
• The **Lodi Dynasty**, part of the Delhi Sultanate, utilized the Iqta system as a key administrative mechanism. Thus, the Iqta and Mansabdari systems cannot be ruled out for the Lodi Dynasty.
 
• The absence of both the Iqta and Mansabdari systems in the **Vijayanagara Empire** confirms that these systems were not prevalent there.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Iqta System:**

 
 
• This system was introduced during the **Delhi Sultanate**, particularly under the rule of **Iltutmish**.
 
• Iqtas were territorial assignments granted to nobles, who were responsible for collecting revenue and maintaining law and order in their regions.
 
• The revenue collected was used for administrative and military purposes, and a portion was sent to the central treasury.
 
• The Iqta system played a significant role in centralizing power and ensuring loyalty among the nobility.
 
 
 
• **Mansabdari System:**
 
 
• Introduced by **Akbar**, this system ranked officials (Mansabdars) based on their military and administrative duties.
 
• Mansabdars were assigned jagirs (land revenue) to maintain troops and manage administration, but the land did not belong to them personally.
 
• This system ensured a strong central control over the empire and reduced the risk of rebellion by nobles.
 
 
 
• **Vijayanagara Empire:**
 
 
• The empire was founded in **1336** by **Harihara I** and **Bukka Raya I**.
 
• It followed the **Nayankara system**, where Nayakas were granted land and were responsible for revenue collection and maintaining military forces.
 
• The rulers of the Vijayanagara Empire focused on decentralization, allowing local governance by Nayakas.
 
• The empire was known for its advancements in art, architecture, and trade, with key contributions in temples such as Hampi.
 
 
 
• **Lodi Dynasty:**
 
 
• The Lodi Dynasty (1451–1526) was the last dynasty of the **Delhi Sultanate**.
 
• They continued using the Iqta system for administrative purposes, ensuring revenue collection and military preparedness.
 
• The dynasty was later overthrown by Babur, leading to the establishment of the Mughal Empire.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Nayankara system** of the Vijayanagara Empire was similar to the feudal system, where Nayakas acted as local governors with military responsibilities.
 
• The **Delhi Sultanate's Iqta system** aimed to centralize power and was a precursor to the Mansabdari system of the Mughals.
 
• The **Vijayanagara Empire** was known for its unique administrative and military systems, which were distinct from the systems of the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal Empire.
 
• The Iqta and Mansabdari systems were crucial in the administration of the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal Empire but were not adopted by the Vijayanagara rulers.

__
 
• **The Battle of Haldighati** was fought on **18 June 1576**, between the forces of **Akbar**, led by **Man Singh I of Amber**, and **Maharana Pratap**, the ruler of Mewar.
 
• The battle is regarded as one of the most significant conflicts in Indian history as it symbolized the resistance of Rajputs against Mughal dominance.
 
• **Maharana Pratap** fought valiantly with his army despite being outnumbered by the Mughal forces. His loyal horse, **Chetak**, is remembered for its bravery during the battle.
 
• The battle was indecisive, but the Mughals claimed a tactical victory as Maharana Pratap had to retreat. However, he continued to resist Mughal rule throughout his life.
 
• The battlefield of Haldighati is located near **Gogunda**, in the present-day state of **Rajasthan**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Maharana Pratap:**

 
 
• Maharana Pratap was born on **9 May 1540**, in **Kumbhalgarh, Mewar**.
 
• He is remembered for his valiant efforts to protect the sovereignty of Mewar against the Mughals.
 
• He adopted guerrilla warfare tactics to harass and weaken the Mughal forces over time.
 
• His legacy continues to inspire Indians as a symbol of patriotism and bravery.
 
 
 
• **Akbar:**
 
 
• Akbar was the third Mughal emperor who ruled India from **1556 to 1605**.
 
• He aimed to expand his empire and bring Rajput kingdoms under Mughal control.
 
• Known for his policy of **religious tolerance**, Akbar sought alliances with Rajput rulers through diplomacy and marriages.
 
 
 
• **Man Singh I:**
 
 
• Man Singh I, a trusted general of Akbar, led the Mughal forces during the Battle of Haldighati.
 
• He was the ruler of **Amber** (modern-day Jaipur) and played a key role in the Mughal administration.
 
 
 
• **Chetak:**
 
 
• Chetak, Maharana Pratap's horse, is celebrated for its loyalty and courage during the Battle of Haldighati.
 
• The horse sustained injuries while protecting Maharana Pratap but ensured his escape from the battlefield before succumbing to its wounds.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Battle:**
 
 
• The battle highlighted the fierce resistance of regional powers like Mewar against the centralized Mughal authority.
 
• It underscored the importance of guerrilla tactics in asymmetric warfare.
 
• Despite losing the battle, Maharana Pratap's unwavering spirit is celebrated as a hallmark of Indian pride and resilience.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Battle of Haldighati** is often romanticized in Indian folklore and literature, portraying Maharana Pratap as a national hero.
 
• Maharana Pratap never accepted Mughal supremacy, and his resistance laid the groundwork for future freedom struggles in India.
 
• The battle is commemorated annually at the Haldighati battlefield, which has become a historical site and a symbol of Rajput valor.
 
• Akbar’s strategy of diplomacy and warfare to consolidate his empire was challenged by leaders like Maharana Pratap, showcasing the resistance of regional powers.

question: Which of the following indicates the system introduced by Lord Cornwallis granting legal ownership of land to the zamindars in Bengal in order to get a fixed revenue by a fixed date?
solution:
The correct answer is __**The Permanent Settlement**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Permanent Settlement system**, also known as the **Zamindari system**, was implemented by **Lord Cornwallis in 1793** to **confer legal ownership of land to zamindars in Bengal.**
 
• Under this arrangement, zamindars were designated **as the landowners**, and an agreement was reached between the company and the zamindars to fix the land revenue.
 
• In this system, the government retained **10/11th of the total land revenue collected **by the zamindars, while the remaining portion was retained by the zamindars themselves.
 
• The Permanent Settlement system was predominantly observed in regions such as **West Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, and Madhya Pradesh.**
 
• It provided zamindars with perpetual land rights, without stipulating fixed rent or occupancy rights for actual cultivators. Consequently, zamindars were tasked with collecting land revenue from the farmers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The Ryotwari system,** introduced in 1820 in British India, was a land revenue system.
 
• **The ****Mahalwari system**, introduced in 1822 by Holt Mackenzie, was a land revenue system.
 
• **The Taluqdari System** was developed as a fiscal policy and a zamindari management technique.

• Following his conquest of the Deccan, Akbar further expanded his administrative divisions, establishing three additional subahs: Berar, Khandesh, and Ahmadnagar.

• Akbar ascended to the throne after his father, Humayun, and was initially supported by a regent,
 
• Bairam Khan, who aided in expanding and consolidating Mughal territories in the Indian subcontinent.
 
• Under Akbar's rule, Mughal India experienced significant economic growth, tripling in both size and wealth, which facilitated commercial expansion and fostered the flourishing of an Indo-Persian culture.
 
• Following Akbar's reign, his son, Prince Salim, later known as Jahangir, succeeded him as emperor.

question: The Fatwa-i-Alamgiri, a major compilation of Islamic law, was commissioned by:
solution:
The correct answer is __**Aurangzeb**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Fatwa-i-Alamgiri** is a comprehensive compilation of Islamic laws and jurisprudence in the Hanafi school of thought.
 
• This monumental work was commissioned by **Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb**, who reigned over India from 1658 to 1707.
 
• Aurangzeb ordered the compilation to ensure uniformity in the application of Islamic law across his vast empire.
 
• The work was compiled by a team of prominent Islamic scholars, including **Sheikh Nizam Burhanpuri** and **Qazi Shaikh-ul-Islam**, under the direct supervision of Aurangzeb.
 
• The Fatwa-i-Alamgiri was written in **Arabic** and later translated into **Persian**, serving as a legal manual for qazis (judges) and administrators in the empire.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Shah Jahan**:

 
 
• Shah Jahan (reigned 1628–1658) was known for his patronage of art and architecture, particularly the construction of the **Taj Mahal** in memory of his wife, Mumtaz Mahal.
 
• He focused on architectural achievements rather than legal or religious reform.
 
• His reign is often referred to as the Golden Age of Mughal architecture.
 
 
 
• **Akbar**:
 
 
• Akbar (reigned 1556–1605) was known for his policy of religious tolerance and the establishment of the **Din-i-Ilahi** (a syncretic religion).
 
• He commissioned the creation of the **Ain-i-Akbari** and **Akbarnama**, which documented the administrative and cultural aspects of his empire.
 
• Unlike Aurangzeb, Akbar sought to integrate diverse religious communities rather than enforce Islamic law exclusively.
 
 
 
• **Jahangir**:
 
 
• Jahangir (reigned 1605–1627) was known for his keen interest in art, culture, and nature.
 
• He authored the **Jahangirnama**, an autobiographical account of his reign.
 
• His reign was marked by relative stability, but he did not focus on legal or religious codification like Aurangzeb.
 
 
 
• **Fatwa-i-Alamgiri**:
 
 
• The Fatwa-i-Alamgiri was a key legal text that codified Islamic jurisprudence and became a reference for qazis during Aurangzeb’s reign.
 
• It addressed various aspects of governance, criminal law, family matters, and commerce, ensuring consistency in legal administration.
 
• The work reflects Aurangzeb’s commitment to Islamic orthodoxy and his emphasis on Sharia law in governance.

question: In which year did Babur take control of Kabul?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1504 CE**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Babur, the founder of the Mughal Empire in India, captured Kabul in **1504 CE**, marking a significant milestone in his career.
 
• At the time, Babur was only 21 years old and faced challenges due to his expulsion from his ancestral home in Ferghana (modern-day Uzbekistan).
 
• Taking control of Kabul provided Babur with a strategic base to consolidate his power and plan future expeditions into India.
 
• Kabul acted as a political and military center for Babur, enabling him to gather resources, troops, and allies for his campaigns.
 
• Babur’s conquest of Kabul was critical in his eventual establishment of the Mughal Empire in India after the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: 1500 CE**

 
 
• While Babur was active during this period, he was still struggling to establish his authority in Central Asia.
 
• He did not capture Kabul in 1500 CE but was involved in conflicts around Ferghana and Samarkand.
 
 
 
• **Option 2: 1508 CE**
 
 
• By 1508 CE, Babur had already consolidated his rule over Kabul and was planning further campaigns into northern India.
 
• During this time, Babur focused on strengthening his position in Afghanistan and surrounding areas.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: 1512 CE**
 
 
• In 1512 CE, Babur attempted to regain control of Samarkand but was defeated by the Uzbeks under Muhammad Shaybani Khan.
 
• This event was significant in Babur’s life but unrelated to his conquest of Kabul, which had already occurred years earlier.
 
 
 
• **Main Theme: Babur’s Early Career**
 
 
• Babur was a descendant of Timur on his father’s side and Genghis Khan on his mother’s side, giving him a rich lineage of conquerors.
 
• His early career was marked by hardships, including losing his kingdom in Ferghana and struggling to regain political power.
 
• Capturing Kabul in 1504 CE was a turning point that allowed Babur to rebuild his fortunes and eventually pave the way for the establishment of the Mughal Empire.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The title "Zinda Pir" or "Living Saint"** was attributed to **Aurangzeb**, the sixth Mughal emperor of India.
 
• Aurangzeb was known for his **piety and strict adherence to Islamic principles**, which earned him this title.
 
• He was highly devout and carried out his religious duties with dedication, which included performing regular prayers and fasting.
 
• Aurangzeb was also known for his personal simplicity and ascetic lifestyle, avoiding indulgence in the luxurious lifestyle often associated with Mughal emperors.
 
• His commitment to religion and moral conduct led his followers to regard him as a saintly figure, thereby calling him "Zinda Pir."

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Aurangzeb:**

 
 
• Born on **3 November 1618**, Aurangzeb was the son of Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal.
 
• He ruled from **1658 to 1707**, making him the longest-reigning Mughal emperor.
 
• He expanded the Mughal Empire to its greatest territorial extent, covering almost the entire Indian subcontinent.
 
• Aurangzeb is remembered for his **religious orthodoxy** and implementation of Islamic laws, such as the reimposition of the Jizya tax on non-Muslims.
 
• Despite his religious fervor, his policies were controversial, leading to dissent among certain communities and regions.
 
 
 
• **Other Mughal Emperors:**
 
 
• **Akbar:** Known as "Akbar the Great," he ruled from **1556 to 1605**. Akbar was famous for his policy of religious tolerance and his efforts to integrate diverse cultures within the empire.
 
• **Babur:** The founder of the Mughal Empire, Babur ruled from **1526 to 1530**. He was known for his military conquests and establishing Mughal rule in India.
 
• **Jahangir:** Jahangir ruled from **1605 to 1627**. He was known for his love for art, nature, and his administrative reforms.
 
 
 
• **Religious Policies of Aurangzeb:**
 
 
• Aurangzeb's reign was marked by his strict adherence to Islamic principles, including the enforcement of Sharia law.
 
• He banned practices that he deemed un-Islamic, such as music and certain festivals, which led to criticism from various sections of society.
 
• Despite his policies, he maintained a vast and efficient administrative system that contributed to the empire's prosperity.
 
 
 
• **Legacy:**
 
 
• Aurangzeb's legacy remains a subject of debate among historians due to his religious orthodoxy and administrative policies.
 
• While he expanded the empire and maintained strict governance, his policies alienated certain communities, leading to resistance and eventual weakening of the Mughal Empire after his death in **1707**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Aurangzeb's title "Zinda Pir"** is indicative of his personal religious devotion rather than his political or administrative achievements.
 
• His reign saw significant military expansion but also laid the groundwork for the eventual decline of the Mughal Empire due to his rigid policies.
 
• Despite controversies, Aurangzeb's ascetic lifestyle and devout practices left a lasting impression on the cultural and religious history of India.

subject: GK
question: Which Mughal emperor prohibited the practice of Sati and issued farmans to that effect?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Akbar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Akbar**, the third Mughal Emperor, is known for his progressive reforms, including the prohibition of the practice of **Sati**. Sati was a social custom wherein a widow immolated herself on her husband’s funeral pyre.
 
• Akbar issued **farmans** (royal edicts) to discourage and prohibit the practice of Sati, showing his commitment to improving the social status of women in his empire.
 
• He allowed Sati only when the widow gave her **full consent**, free of any external pressure, and even then, it was discouraged by his administration.
 
• These measures were part of Akbar's broader policy of **social reforms**, aimed at promoting tolerance and humanity in his rule.
 
• Akbar’s reign (1556–1605) was marked by his efforts to create a more inclusive and harmonious society by addressing various regressive practices and customs prevalent during that period.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **About Akbar:**

 
 
• Akbar, known as **Akbar the Great**, was one of the most illustrious rulers of the Mughal Empire and ruled from 1556 to 1605.
 
• He is remembered for his **policy of Sulh-i-Kul** (universal peace), which promoted religious tolerance and harmony among his subjects.
 
• Under his reign, Akbar abolished discriminatory taxes on non-Muslims, such as the **jizya**, and encouraged interfaith dialogues.
 
 
 
• **Sati Practice:**
 
 
• **Sati** was a historical practice in which a widow immolated herself on her deceased husband's funeral pyre. It was prevalent in some parts of India, particularly among the upper caste Hindu communities.
 
• While Sati was considered an act of devotion by some, it was often forced upon widows, leading to significant human rights abuses.
 
• Akbar was among the first rulers to take **concrete steps** to curb this practice through his royal edicts.
 
 
 
• **Other Mughal Emperors:**
 
 
• **Babur:** The founder of the Mughal Empire, Babur (1526–1530), focused on establishing his rule in India and did not implement significant social reforms.
 
• **Humayun:** Akbar’s father, Humayun (1530–1540, 1555–1556), had a short and tumultuous reign, leaving little scope for social reforms.
 
• **Aurangzeb:** The last prominent Mughal emperor, Aurangzeb (1658–1707), is known for his orthodox and conservative policies, which contrasted with Akbar's liberal approach.
 
 
 
• **Further Efforts to Abolish Sati:**
 
 
• The practice of Sati was officially abolished during British rule in **1829** by Governor-General **Lord William Bentinck**, with significant support from social reformers like **Raja Ram Mohan Roy**.
 
• Raja Ram Mohan Roy was instrumental in advocating against Sati, highlighting its inhumanity and pushing for legal reforms.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Akbar’s Social Reforms:**

 
 
• Akbar introduced several progressive reforms, including banning child marriage and promoting widow remarriage.
 
• He established the **Ibadat Khana** (House of Worship) at Fatehpur Sikri to hold discussions with scholars of various religions.
 
• Akbar’s reforms extended to taxation policies as well, with the introduction of the **Din-i-Ilahi** to foster unity among his subjects.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Akbar’s Reforms:**
 
 
• Akbar’s efforts to curb Sati and other regressive practices reflect his visionary leadership and commitment to creating a just and humane society.
 
• These reforms laid the foundation for subsequent rulers and reformers to address social injustices in India.

question: The first Mughal Emperor to be buried outside India.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Babur**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Babur**, the founder of the **Mughal Empire** in the Indian subcontinent, was the first emperor of the dynasty to be buried outside the borders of modern-day **India**.
 
• After defeating **Ibrahim Lodi** in the **First Battle of Panipat** in **1526**, he established his rule in North India but died shortly after in **Agra** on **December 26, 1530**.
 
• Initially, his body was interred in the **Aram Bagh** (Garden of Rest) in **Agra**, situated on the banks of the **Yamuna River**.
 
• However, **Babur** had expressed a strong sentimental desire in his autobiography, the **Baburnama**, to be buried in his favorite city, **Kabul**, in **Afghanistan**.
 
• During the reign of either **Sher Shah Suri** or his son **Humayun** (around **1539–1544**), his remains were moved to the **Bagh-e Babur** (Gardens of Babur) in **Kabul**.
 
• His tomb is located in a **Charbagh** (four-fold garden) layout, which became a signature architectural style for future **Mughal** mausoleums.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Humayun**:

 
 
• The second **Mughal** emperor is buried in **Delhi**. His tomb is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** and was the first major **Mughal** structure to use red sandstone on such a large scale.
 
 
 
• **Akbar**:
 
 
• The third emperor, **Akbar the Great**, is buried in a magnificent tomb at **Sikandra**, located on the outskirts of **Agra**.
 
 
 
• **Shah Jahan**:
 
 
• The fifth emperor is buried in the **Taj Mahal** in **Agra**, placed next to his beloved wife, **Mumtaz Mahal**.
 
 
 
• **Other Emperors Buried Outside India**:
 
 
• **Jahangir** was buried in **Shahdara Bagh** in **Lahore**, **Pakistan**.
 
• **Bahadur Shah Zafar**, the last **Mughal** emperor, was exiled by the British and buried in **Yangon**, **Myanmar**.

question: The Mughal Emperor who abolished the Jizya tax in 1564 was:
solution:
The correct answer is __**Akbar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Akbar**, the third **Mughal Emperor**, is renowned for his policies of **religious tolerance** and administrative innovations that aimed to unify a diverse Indian population.
 
• In **1564**, he officially abolished the **Jizya tax**, which was a per capita tax levied on non-Muslim subjects, known as **dhimmis**, living under Islamic rule.
 
• This significant reform was rooted in **Akbar’s** philosophy of **Sulh-i-kul** (universal peace), which sought to provide equal status to all citizens regardless of their religious beliefs.
 
• The abolition of **Jizya** followed his decision in **1563** to end the **Pilgrimage Tax**, a levy on Hindus visiting holy sites, further consolidating his image as a liberal and secular monarch.
 
• By removing these financial burdens, **Akbar** secured the loyalty of the **Rajputs** and the broader **Hindu majority**, which was essential for the expansion and stability of the **Mughal Empire**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Humayun**:

 
 
• The second **Mughal Emperor** and father of **Akbar**, whose reign was primarily defined by his struggle to reclaim the throne from the **Sur Dynasty**.
 
 
 
• **Jahangir**:
 
 
• The fourth **Mughal Emperor** who largely continued his father’s inclusive policies but is most noted for his patronage of **Mughal art** and his memoirs, **Tuzuk-e-Jahangiri**.
 
 
 
• **Shah Jahan**:
 
 
• The fifth **Mughal Emperor**, famous for the construction of the **Taj Mahal** and the **Peacock Throne**, though the status of Jizya remained unchanged during his peak years.
 
 
 
• **Aurangzeb**:
 
 
• The sixth **Mughal Emperor** who eventually reversed **Akbar’s** policy by re-imposing the **Jizya tax** in **1679**, leading to significant socio-political friction.

__
 
• **Fahien**, the renowned Chinese Buddhist monk and traveler, visited India during the reign of **Chandragupta II**, also known as **Vikramaditya**. This period is considered one of the golden ages of Indian history.
 
• Fahien traveled to India in the early **5th century CE**, specifically during the reign of Chandragupta II, between **375–415 CE**.
 
• During his travels, Fahien documented the prosperity, religious tolerance, and administrative excellence of the Gupta Empire under Chandragupta II.
 
• He visited important cities such as **Pataliputra**, **Mathura**, and **Kanchipuram**, as well as Buddhist sites like **Lumbini** and **Sarnath**.
 
• Fahien's travel accounts, documented in his book **"Record of Buddhist Kingdoms"**, provide valuable insights into the socio-political and cultural aspects of India during the Gupta period.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Chandragupta II:**

 
 
• Chandragupta II, also known as **Vikramaditya**, was one of the most successful rulers of the Gupta Empire.
 
• His reign marked significant achievements in **art, architecture, science, and literature**, contributing to the Gupta Empire's golden age.
 
• Under his rule, India saw substantial economic prosperity, cultural growth, and religious tolerance.
 
• He expanded his empire through strategic alliances and military conquests, including defeating the **Saka rulers** in western India.
 
• Chandragupta II established **Ujjain** as an important political and cultural center.
 
 
 
• **Fahien's Travels:**
 
 
• Fahien embarked on his journey to India in search of **Buddhist scriptures** and to study the religion's practices and teachings.
 
• He spent several years in India, visiting monasteries, temples, and universities like the renowned **Nalanda University**.
 
• Fahien praised the administrative efficiency of the Gupta Empire and its commitment to justice and welfare.
 
• He noted that the people of India lived in harmony, and the rulers were benevolent, emphasizing the absence of capital punishment during Chandragupta II's reign.
 
• Fahien's accounts also highlight the flourishing trade and economic activities during the Gupta period.
 
 
 
• **Gupta Empire:**
 
 
• The Gupta Empire is often referred to as the **Golden Age of India** due to its remarkable achievements in various fields.
 
• It was known for advancements in **mathematics** (concept of zero), **astronomy**, **medicine**, and **literature**.
 
• The empire promoted religious tolerance, and both Hinduism and Buddhism flourished under its rule.
 
• Trade and commerce were highly developed, with India being a major player in the **Silk Road trade network**.
 
• The Gupta rulers were patrons of art and culture, resulting in the construction of magnificent temples and sculptures.
 
 
 
• **Other Options:**
 
 
• **Kumaragupta:** He ruled after Chandragupta II and was known for establishing the **Nalanda University**. However, Fahien did not visit India during his reign.
 
• **Samudragupta:** Chandragupta II's father, renowned for his military conquests and cultural patronage. Fahien visited India after Samudragupta's reign.
 
• **Chandragupta I:** He was the founder of the Gupta Empire but ruled before Fahien's travels to India.

• His observations highlight the significance of Buddhism in India and its spread to other parts of Asia.
 
• Chandragupta II's reign is regarded as a high point in Indian history for its contributions to culture, science, and administration.
 
• The Gupta Empire's influence extended to Southeast Asia, shaping the region's art, culture, and political systems.

subject: GK
question: The term "Amaram" in Vijayanagara administration was associated with:
solution:
The correct answer is __**Military fief**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The term **Amaram** in the Vijayanagara administration referred to a **military fief**, which means a land grant assigned to commanders or military officers in place of their services.
 
• The **Amaram** system was primarily utilized to organize and maintain a strong military structure in the Vijayanagara Empire.
 
• Under this system, the Amara Nayakas (military commanders) were given land grants called "Amaram," and in return, they had to maintain a specified number of troops ready for the empire's defense or campaigns.
 
• The Amara Nayakas had administrative control over the land and were allowed to collect revenue from it, which was then used to fund their military obligations.
 
• This system played a crucial role in decentralizing the military and administrative responsibilities, ensuring effective governance across the vast Vijayanagara Empire.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Vijayanagara Empire:**

 
 
• The Vijayanagara Empire was established in **1336 CE** by **Harihara I** and **Bukka Raya I**. It was one of the most powerful South Indian kingdoms.
 
• The empire is renowned for its contributions to **art, architecture**, and **administration**, as well as its ability to maintain a strong military.
 
• The capital city of the empire was **Hampi**, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
 
 
 
• **Amara Nayaka System:**
 
 
• This system was inspired by the **Iqta system** of the Delhi Sultanate but was adapted to suit the needs of the Vijayanagara Empire.
 
• Amara Nayakas were responsible for **revenue collection**, **maintenance of law and order**, and providing military support to the central authority.
 
• They acted as intermediaries between the central government and the local population.
 
 
 
• **Other Administrative Systems:**
 
 
• The Vijayanagara administration was highly decentralized, with a well-organized structure involving provincial governors and local chieftains.
 
• The empire also maintained a detailed system of land measurement and revenue collection.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other Systems:**
 
 
• Unlike the Amaram system, a **tax exemption** was generally associated with religious or charitable grants in the form of **Brahmadeya** or **Devadana** lands.
 
• Land redistribution was not a significant feature of the Vijayanagara administration, but was seen in later agrarian reforms in India.

question: Lord Hastings initiated the ______ where the East India Company claimed that its authority was supreme and hence its power was greater than that of Indian states
solution:
The correct answer is __**Policy of ‘Paramountcy**__**’.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **__Important Points__**

__
 
• Lord Hastings, who was the Governor-General of India from 1813 to 1823, introduced a new policy of 'paramountcy'.
 
• By this policy, the Company claimed that its authority was paramount or supreme, hence its power was greater than that of Indian states.
 
• The **chief instrument through which Lord Dalhousie** implemented his policy of annexation was the** ‘Doctrine of Lapse’**.
 
 
• Under the Doctrine of Lapse, when the ruler of a protected state died without a natural heir, his/her state was not to pass to an adopted heir as sanctioned by the age-old tradition of the country.
 
• Lord Dalhousie came to India as the **Governor-General in 1848**.
 
• **During Lord Canning's tenure “Doctrine of Lapse” was withdrawn**.
 
 
 
• **British Imperial policies** between **1763 and 1776** were focused on **using the colonies to raise revenue** in ways that the colonists saw as **unconstitutional**.
 
 
• 
 
The majority of the colonists were extremely **loyal to the crown** and only became **“reluctant revolutionists” **when there was** no other choice**.

 
 
 

Thus the correct answer is Policy of ‘Paramountcy__’.

question: During the British rule in India, which of the following Governor Generals devised the ‘Doctrine of Lapse’, a policy of annexation?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Lord Dalhousie**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Lord Dalhousie**, Governor-General of the English East India Company from **1848 to 1856,** instituted the **Doctrine of Lapse,** an annexation strategy across the Indian subcontinent.
 
• Under this policy, the Company would **absorb territories** under the subsidiary alliance if the ruling authority failed to leave a natural heir.
 
• This facilitated the Company's acquisition of regions governed by rulers without successors.
 
• The Doctrine remained in effect until 1858, following the transition from Company rule to the British Raj under direct Crown administration.
 
• **Elements of the Doctrine **persisted in Indian governance, used to discontinue recognition of individual princely families until 1971, when the Indira Gandhi administration ceased acknowledgment of former ruling dynasties.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **James Andrew Broun-Ramsay, **1st Marquess of Dalhousie, previously known as the **Earl of Dalhousie** from **1838 to 1849, **was a prominent Scottish statesman and colonial administrator during the British Raj in India.
 
• Serving as **Governor-General from 1848 to 1856**, he left a lasting legacy on the Indian subcontinent. His contributions to the colonial educational system were significant, as he expanded its scope to include mass education alongside elite higher education.
 
• Dalhousie's reforms extended beyond education; he introduced passenger trains to the railway network, implemented the electric telegraph system, and standardized postage rates, labeling them as the "three great engines of social improvement."
 
• Additionally, he established the **Public Works Department** in India. Dalhousie's tenure as Governor-General is characterized by his forward-thinking approach, which consolidated East India Company rule in India and laid the groundwork for subsequent administrations.
 
• His strategic policies played a crucial role in quelling potential rebellions, providing stability for future governance in the region.

 __

subject: GK
question:
The "Subsidiary Alliance" system, pioneered by Lord Wellesley, had a significant impact on the political map of India.

What was a primary consequence for the Indian states that entered into this alliance?

options.text: They gained greater military strength and autonomy in their external relations.
They were effectively brought under British political influence and control, losing their independent foreign policy and often their military capacity.
They experienced rapid economic growth due to British investment and administrative reforms.
They formed a strong unified front against the expansion of British power in India.

solution:
The correct answer is __**They were effectively brought under British political influence and control, losing their independent foreign policy and often their military capacity.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Subsidiary Alliance** was a policy introduced by **Lord Wellesley**, the Governor-General of India from 1798 to 1805. Its primary aim was to bring Indian princely states under British control.
 
• Under this system, Indian rulers were required to accept a permanent stationing of a **British military contingent** in their territory, ostensibly for their protection. However, they had to bear the cost of maintaining this force.
 
• The Indian states entering the alliance **lost their autonomy in foreign affairs**. They were prohibited from forming alliances with other powers or waging wars without British consent.
 
• Many states also had to disband their own armies, which effectively reduced their military capacity and made them dependent on the British for defense.
 
• The policy led to the **political subjugation** of Indian states. While they retained nominal sovereignty, their rulers were essentially puppets of the British administration.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Key Characteristics of Subsidiary Alliance:**

 
 
• The alliance was primarily used as a political tool to expand British influence and control over Indian territories.
 
• The Indian rulers had to pay a subsidy to the British for the maintenance of the stationed British troops.
 
• If the subsidy could not be paid, parts of the ruler’s territory were annexed by the British, as seen in the case of Awadh.
 
 
 
• **Notable States under the Subsidiary Alliance:**
 
 
• The **Nizam of Hyderabad** was the first to accept the Subsidiary Alliance in 1798.
 
• Other states like Mysore, Awadh, and the Maratha states also entered into the alliance under increasing British pressure.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Subsidiary Alliance:**
 
 
• It marked the beginning of indirect British rule over large parts of India, consolidating the British Empire in the subcontinent.
 
• Indian rulers faced a loss of sovereignty, which eventually led to widespread discontent and contributed to the **First War of Independence in 1857**.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Other British Policies:**
 
 
• The Subsidiary Alliance was followed by the **Doctrine of Lapse**, another policy aimed at annexing princely states lacking legitimate heirs.
 
• While the Doctrine of Lapse directly annexed territories, the Subsidiary Alliance maintained a facade of local rule but with British control over key aspects of governance.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Lord Wellesley’s Vision:**

 
 
• Wellesley aimed to create a buffer zone of dependent states around British territories to protect them from French or other European colonial powers.
 
• This policy was also a response to the growing influence of Napoleon Bonaparte in Europe during this period.
 
 
 
• **Long-term Consequences:**
 
 
• The Subsidiary Alliance weakened the Indian princely states economically and militarily, paving the way for direct British annexation in the future.
 
• By controlling the military and foreign policies of Indian states, the British ensured their dominance without immediate direct administration.

__
 
• India was divided into India and Pakistan by the **India Independence Act, 1947.**
 
• India Independence Act, 1947 was an Act of the British Parliament that partitioned India into two dominions of **India and Pakistan**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **The Mountbatten Plan or the 3 June Plan-**
 
 
• The June 3 plan, also known as the Mountbatten Plan included these principles:-
 
 

 
• The principle of the partition of British India was accepted by the British Government
 
• Successor governments would be given dominion status
 
• Autonomy and sovereignty to both countries
 
• Can make their own constitution.

 
• **Features of India Independence Act, 1947-**

 
 
• **Division of British India into the two new dominions of India and Pakistan**, with effect from August 15, 1947.
 
• **Partition of the provinces of Bengal and Punjab** between the two new countries.
 
• Establishment of the** office of Governor-General** in each of the two new countries, as representatives of the Crown.
 
• Conferral of **complete legislative authority upon the respective Constituent Assemblies** of the two new countries.
 
• **Termination of British suzerainty over the princely states**, with effect from 15 August 1947, and recognised the **right of states to remain independent or accede to either dominion.**
 
• **Abolition of the use of the title "Emperor of India"** by the British monarch.
 
• The Act also made provision for the **division of joint property,** etc. between the two new countries, including in particular the division of the armed forces.

__
 
• **The Charter Act of 1833** marked a significant milestone in Indian legal history by **instituting a Law Commission** tasked **with the consolidation and codification of Indian laws.**
 
• Established in 1834, the inaugural Law Commission was helmed by TB Macaulay.
 
• Under Macaulay's leadership, the commission's recommendations paved the way for the formalization of the Criminal Procedure Code and the penal code, laying the groundwork for a more organized legal framework in India.
 
• Furthermore, the Charter Act of 1833 heralded a pivotal shift in India's administrative landscape by opening up avenues for Indian participation.
 
• It mandated that government employment be allocated based on merit rather than factors such as race, religion, color, or birth, signaling a move towards a more inclusive and equitable governance structure.
 
• Subsequently, the Charter Act of 1853 saw the establishment of the second Law Commission in England, commencing its operations in the same year. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The Indian Councils Act of 1909,** passed by the British Parliament, initiated some reforms in the legislative councils and partially expanded Indian involvement in the governance of British India.
 
• **The Government of India (GOI) Act of 1919 **marked a significant step by the administration towards the eventual introduction of responsible government in India, marking a pivotal moment in its governance.
 
• **The Charter Act of 1813,** also referred to as the East India Company Act of 1813, was legislation enacted by the British Parliament to renew the charter of the British East India Company for an additional 20 years.

question: The Arms Act was passed in _____ that prevented Indians from keeping arms without an appropriate license.
solution:
The Correct Answer is __**1878**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Arms Act**

 
 
• Between 1876 and 1880, Lord Lytton held the position of Viceroy of India.
 
• He approved both the 1878** Arms Act** and the Vernacular Press** Act.**
 
• The** Arms** Act was developed by the British during the 19th century in response to the rising Indian nationalism.
 
• It became law in 1878.
 
• The production and sale of fir**earms** in the nation were controlled by this statute.
 
• No Indian was permitted to produce, market, or even possess a weapon without first obtaining a government permission.
 
• The British intended to prevent Indians from possessing rifles and pistols because they did not want another uprising like the one that occurred in 1857 CE.
 
• The act underwent significant amendments in **1959 and 1983**, but there was no specific amendment that disallowed Indians from possessing arms.
 
• However, in **1962**, the Indian government passed the Defence of India Rules, which prohibited the possession of arms and ammunition by any person without a valid license.
 
• **This law was enacted during the Indo-China** War to prevent unauthorized persons from possessing arms that could be used against the country's interests.
 
• In **1983**, the Arms Act was amended to further regulate the **possession of firearms and ammunition in the country**.
 
• The amendment tightened the licensing requirements and imposed stricter penalties for** violations of the law.****​**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lord Litton****​**

 
 
• Edward Robert Lytton Bulwer-Lytton, 1st Earl of Lytton, also known as Lord Lytton, was an English politician who was Viceroy of India from 1876 to 1880.
 
• The first Famine Commission was set up in 1878 under the Chairmanship of Sir Richard Strachey. The commission recommended state interference in food trade in the event of famine. India witnessed another major famine in 1896-97.
 
• Lytton's viceroyalty was characterized by ruthlessness in both domestic and foreign affairs.
 
• At the time, India was in the grip of a famine caused by crop failure in 1876. In response, he called a **Durbar and declared Queen Victoria to be the "Empress of India".**
 
• Vernacular Press Act**(1878**)​
 
 
• People were dissatisfied with Lytton's unpopular policies, and the native vernacular press mocked him. He drafted the Vernacular Press Act to curtail the wings of the Vernacular Press.
 
• By virtue of this act, District Magistrates were empowered, without prior permission from the government, to compel a printer and publisher of any kind to enter into a bond, undertaking not to publish anything that might incite discontent against the government.
 
• The magistrate was also given the authority to deposit security, which could be confiscated if the printer violated the bond.
 
• If the printer violates this again, his press may be seized.

• **Government of India Act 1858** was the legislation that marked the end of the East India Company's rule in India and transferred the control of India to the British Crown.
 
• This act was enacted in response to the Indian Rebellion of 1857, which exposed the vulnerabilities and inadequacies of the Company's administration.
 
• Under this Act, the British government established the office of the Secretary of State for India, who was given complete authority and control over the Indian administration.
 
• The Act also led to the creation of the India Council to assist the Secretary of State for India.

• The Act was also known as the Act for the Better Government of India and was passed on August 2, 1858.
 
• It led to the establishment of the office of Viceroy of India, a position held by the Governor-General of India, who acted as the representative of the British Crown.
 
• The Act aimed to improve the governance of India by ensuring a more direct and accountable administration under the British Parliament.
 
• The administrative structure set up by this Act remained largely unchanged until the passage of the Government of India Act 1935, which introduced provincial autonomy and federal structure.

question: How many members (elected and nominated) were there in the Council of State under the Government of India Act 1919 passed by the Parliament of the United Kingdom to expand participation of Indians in the government of India?
solution:
The correct answer is **__60.__**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Government of India Act 1919 **, established the **Council of State as the upper house of bicameral legislature in India.**
 
• Th**e Council of State had 60 members, 34 elected and 26 nominated member**s, with **tenure of five years.**
 
• The GOI Act 1919 was based on the **recommendations of Edwin Montagu**, the Secretary of State for India and **Lord Chelmsford**, the Viceroy of India.
 
• So, GOI Act 1919 also known as** Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__****GOI Act 1919, Important Facts:**

 
• **Diarchy**:

 
 
• Introduced diarchy in provinces with divided subjects (Transferred to Indian ministers, Reserved under British control).
 
 
 
• **Bicameral Legislature**:
 
 
• Established two houses at the Centre: Council of State (Upper House) and Legislative Assembly (Lower House).
 
 
 
• **Expanded Provincial Councils**:
 
 
• Increased the number of elected Indian members in provincial councils.
 
 
 
• **Limited Franchise**:
 
 
• Expanded, but limited suffrage based on property and educational qualifications.
 
• Voting rights extended to some women under restrictive conditions.
 
 
 
• **Separate Electorates**:
 
 
• Continued separate electorates for Muslims, Sikhs, and Anglo-Indians.
 
 
 
• **Clear Division**:
 
 
• Demarcation of Central and Provincial subjects.
 
• Provincial subjects split into Transferred and Reserved categories.
 
 
 
• **Governor-General Powers**:
 
 
• Governor-General retained overriding authority over legislative decisions.
 
 
 
• **Public Service Commission**:
 
 
• Introduced the establishment of a Public Service Commission for recruitment.
 
 
 
• **Step Towards Reform**:
 
 
• ​Aimed as a step towards responsible governmenrt, precursor to the 1935 Act.

question:
The "Indian Councils Act of 1892" represented a limited expansion of Indian participation in the legislative councils.

What was a notable feature of this Act regarding the selection of Indian members?

options.text: It introduced universal adult suffrage for the election of Indian members.
It allowed for the direct election of a majority of Indian members to the central legislative council.
It permitted the nomination of some Indian members by the Governor-General and provided for indirect election through electoral colleges.
It mandated equal representation for all religious communities in the legislative councils.

solution:
The correct answer is __**It permitted the nomination of some Indian members by the Governor-General and provided for indirect election through electoral colleges.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Indian Councils Act of 1892 aimed to expand the role of Indians in legislative processes, though in a limited manner.
 
• Under this Act, the Governor-General and provincial governors were permitted to nominate Indian members to the legislative councils.
 
• It introduced the concept of indirect election through electoral colleges, where members were selected by specific groups such as municipalities, district boards, universities, and chambers of commerce.
 
• The nominated and indirectly elected Indian members were given the right to discuss the budget, though not to vote on it.
 
• The Act served as a precursor to later reforms like the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909, which further expanded Indian representation in councils.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: It introduced universal adult suffrage for the election of Indian members**

 
 
• This is incorrect as universal adult suffrage was not introduced until much later in India’s constitutional history, specifically after the enactment of the Constitution of India in 1950.
 
• The 1892 Act only allowed for indirect elections, not direct elections or universal suffrage.
 
 
 
• **Option 2: It allowed for the direct election of a majority of Indian members to the central legislative council**
 
 
• This is incorrect as the Act did not provide for direct elections. Instead, it introduced indirect elections through electoral colleges.
 
• Direct elections were introduced much later during the Government of India Act of 1919 and expanded further in 1935.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: It mandated equal representation for all religious communities in the legislative councils**
 
 
• This is incorrect as the Indian Councils Act of 1892 did not mandate equal representation for all religious communities.
 
• Such provisions were introduced later under the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909, which introduced separate electorates for Muslims.

subject: GK
question: Which system, introduced by the Government of India Act of 1919, classified provincial subjects into "reserved" and "transferred" categories?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Dyarchy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Dyarchy** was introduced under the Government of India Act, 1919, also known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms.
 
• It divided provincial subjects into two categories: **“Reserved” and “Transferred.”**
 
• The **“Reserved” subjects** were to be administered by the Governor and his Executive Council without being accountable to the legislative council. Examples include law and order, finance, and police.
 
• The **“Transferred” subjects** were administered by Indian ministers who were responsible to the legislative councils. Examples include education, public health, and agriculture.
 
• Dyarchy was an attempt to introduce **limited self-governance** in provinces by involving Indians in the administration of transferred subjects while retaining significant powers with the British authorities.
 
• This system remained in effect until it was abolished by the Government of India Act, 1935, which introduced provincial autonomy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Federation**

 
 
• The concept of Federation was proposed in the Government of India Act, 1935.
 
• It aimed to create a federal structure by combining British Indian provinces and princely states into a single political entity.
 
• However, the federal provisions of the Act were not implemented because the princely states were not willing to join the federation.
 
 
 
• **Bicameralism**
 
 
• Bicameralism refers to a legislative system with two houses or chambers, typically an upper house and a lower house.
 
• In India, bicameralism was introduced at the central level by the Government of India Act, 1919, which established a bicameral legislature consisting of the Council of State (Upper House) and the Legislative Assembly (Lower House).
 
• Currently, India follows a bicameral system at the central level (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha) and in some states.
 
 
 
• **Responsible Government**
 
 
• The concept of Responsible Government implies that the executive is responsible to the legislature and ultimately to the people.
 
• In India, the principle of responsible government was fully established with the adoption of the Constitution in 1950.
 
• The Government of India Act, 1935, made a significant move towards responsible government by introducing provincial autonomy.

question: Which of the following correctly describes the responsibilities of Madras and Bombay governors after 1773?

options.text: They operated independently of the Bengal Governor-General.
They had to report to the Governor-General on war, peace, and revenue.
They managed trade but not civil administration.
They were answerable only to the Court of Directors in London.

solution:
The correct answer is __**They had to report to the Governor-General on war, peace, and revenue.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Regulating Act of 1773** was the first step in centralizing British administration in India.
 
• It established the office of the **Governor-General of Bengal**, who held overarching authority over the presidencies of Madras and Bombay.
 
• The governors of Madras and Bombay were required to report to the Governor-General of Bengal on matters related to **war, peace, and revenue**.
 
• This arrangement aimed at ensuring a unified and coordinated approach to governance and resource management across British territories in India.
 
• The Governor-General and his council were also tasked with settling disputes and making decisions in the best interest of the East India Company’s administration.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: They operated independently of the Bengal Governor-General**
 
 
• Before the Regulating Act of 1773, the presidencies of Madras, Bombay, and Bengal operated independently of each other.
 
• However, the act brought the presidencies under the central authority of the Governor-General of Bengal, making this option incorrect.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: They managed trade but not civil administration**
 
 
• While trade was a significant aspect of their responsibilities, the governors of Madras and Bombay were also responsible for civil administration in their regions.
 
• The Regulating Act ensured that their civil and military actions were subject to the oversight of the Governor-General.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: They were answerable only to the Court of Directors in London**
 
 
• While the Court of Directors of the East India Company retained overall supervisory authority, the Regulating Act made the governors of Madras and Bombay answerable to the Governor-General of Bengal for critical matters.
 
• This ensured a hierarchical chain of command within India.
 
 
 
• **Main Theme: The Regulating Act of 1773**
 
 
• The Regulating Act was a landmark piece of legislation introduced by the British Parliament to address administrative inefficiencies and corruption in the East India Company.
 
• It marked the beginning of British control over Indian governance by introducing a centralized system of administration.
 
• The act laid the foundation for subsequent reforms, including the Pitt’s India Act of 1784.

question:
The "Wood's Despatch" of 1854 recommended several significant changes in the Indian education system.

Which of the following was a key recommendation of this despatch?

options.text: The immediate vernacularization of all levels of education.
The establishment of a comprehensive system of education from the primary to the university level, with English as the medium of instruction at higher levels.
The complete privatization of the education sector in India.
The exclusive focus on the training of religious leaders and scholars.

solution:
The correct answer is __**The establishment of a comprehensive system of education from the primary to the university level, with English as the medium of instruction at higher levels.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Wood's Despatch** of **1854** is famously known as the **Magna Carta of English Education in India**, as it was the first document to provide a comprehensive plan for the spread of education.
 
• Prepared by **Sir Charles Wood**, the then President of the **Board of Control**, the despatch was addressed to **Lord Dalhousie**, the Governor-General of India.
 
• It proposed a **structured educational hierarchy** consisting of **Primary Schools** at the bottom, followed by **Middle Schools**, **High Schools**, **Colleges**, and **Universities**.
 
• The despatch recommended that **English** be the medium of instruction for **higher education** (University level) while **vernacular languages** (local mother tongues) be used at the **school level** to ensure wider reach.
 
• It advised the establishment of **Universities** in the presidency towns of **Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras**, modeled after the **University of London**, to regulate and conduct examinations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Administrative Framework**:

 
 
• It recommended the creation of a **Department of Public Instruction (DPI)** in every province to supervise educational activities and maintain standards.
 
 
 
• **Financial Support and Privatization**:
 
 
• To encourage **private enterprise**, the despatch introduced the **Grant-in-Aid system** for private schools that provided **secular education** and met government standards.
 
 
 
• **Social Initiatives**:
 
 
• The document placed significant emphasis on **Women's Education** and **Vocational Training**, advocating for the establishment of **Normal Schools** to train professional teachers.
 
 
 
• **Secular Focus**:
 
 
• It mandated that education in **government-aided institutions** must remain strictly **secular**, although private institutions were allowed to include religious instruction.

• The **Indian Councils Act of 1892** marked a significant milestone in India's legislative history as it allowed for the legislative councils to **discuss the annual budget** for the first time. This was a step towards increasing the role of Indians in legislative processes.
 
• The Act introduced the provision of asking **questions on public matters**, giving members of legislative councils a platform to raise concerns and hold the administration accountable.
 
• Though the Act allowed discussions on the budget, **it did not permit voting on it**, limiting the influence of the councils over financial matters.
 
• The Act also expanded the size of the legislative councils, both at the **central and provincial levels**, thus involving more members in governance.

• **Indian Councils Act, 1892:**

 
 
• This Act was an amendment to the **Indian Councils Act of 1861**.
 
• It allowed for the **non-official members** of the councils to discuss budgetary matters, marking a step towards more inclusive governance.
 
• The councils were expanded in size, and **representation of Indians** was increased, paving the way for further reforms.
 
 
 
• **Key limitations of the Act:**
 
 
• The role of Indians in governance was still largely advisory, with no substantial powers granted to them.
 
• The discussions on the budget were limited to certain parts, and **voting rights were absent**.
 
• The members of the councils were primarily nominated, with only a few being indirectly elected.
 
 
 
• **Subsequent Reforms:**
 
 
• The **Indian Councils Act of 1909** (also known as the Morley-Minto reforms) introduced further changes, such as the inclusion of **separate electorates for Muslims**.
 
• Later, the **Government of India Act of 1919** introduced the concept of diarchy in provinces, granting more administrative powers to Indians.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Act:**
 
 
• The Act of 1892 was an important step in the process of India's **political awakening**.
 
• It laid the foundation for future demands for **self-governance** and greater representation of Indians in legislative bodies.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Role of Legislative Councils:**

 
 
• The legislative councils under the Act were mainly advisory in nature, with their recommendations not binding on the executive.
 
• Despite their limited powers, the councils provided a platform for **Indian leaders** to voice their concerns and grievances.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• The Act was introduced during the tenure of **Lord Dufferin** as the Viceroy of India.
 
• It was a response to the growing demand for **greater representation** and accountability in governance, as voiced by early Indian nationalists.

It did not include any Indian members in its composition, leading to accusations of being an imposition on India's future without Indian representation.
It advocated for the strengthening of the system of separate electorates.

solution:
The correct answer is __**It did not include any Indian members in its composition, leading to accusations of being an imposition on India's future without Indian representation.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Simon Commission** was appointed in **1927** to review the working of the Government of India Act, 1919, and suggest further constitutional reforms in India. However, the commission did not include **any Indian members**, which made it highly controversial and unacceptable to Indian leaders.
 
• The exclusion of Indians was seen as a direct disregard for Indian participation in deciding their own political future. This led to widespread protests by leaders across political and social spectrums. **Hence, this was the primary reason for the boycott.**
 
• On its arrival in India in **1928**, the Simon Commission faced demonstrations with slogans such as **"Simon Go Back."** This highlighted the level of public discontent.
 
• The boycott of the Simon Commission united various factions of the Indian political landscape, including the **Indian National Congress**, the **Muslim League**, and other regional parties, in their opposition to the commission's composition.
 
• The protests also led to tragic incidents like the lathi charge on **Lala Lajpat Rai** during a demonstration in Lahore, which later resulted in his death. This further fueled anti-British sentiments across the country.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Government of India Act, 1919:**

 
 
• Also known as the **Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms**, this act introduced dyarchy at the provincial level, dividing subjects into "transferred" and "reserved" categories.
 
• The act was criticized for not granting sufficient autonomy to Indians, which formed the backdrop for the need to review its progress through the Simon Commission.
 
 
 
• **Simon Commission's Recommendations:**
 
 
• Despite being boycotted, the Simon Commission suggested the abolition of dyarchy and the establishment of a **federation of British India and princely states.**
 
• The recommendations later influenced the framing of the **Government of India Act, 1935**, which introduced provincial autonomy and other reforms.
 
 
 
• **Key Leaders and Their Role:**
 
 
• The Indian National Congress, under leaders like **Motilal Nehru** and **Jawaharlal Nehru**, played a pivotal role in organizing protests against the commission.
 
• The **Muslim League**, despite its ideological differences with the Congress, also opposed the Simon Commission, showing a rare moment of unity.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Protests:**
 
 
• The protests against the Simon Commission were significant in uniting Indians across political and social lines against British imperialism.
 
• It paved the way for the **Nehru Report** in 1928, which was an Indian effort to draft a constitution for self-governance.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• The commission's exclusion of Indians highlighted the colonial administration's disregard for Indian aspirations and further intensified the demand for **Swaraj** (self-rule).
 
• The slogan **"Simon Go Back"** became a symbol of resistance and galvanized the youth and working class of India against British policies.

subject: GK
question:
​​The "Rowlatt Acts" of 1919 faced intense opposition from Indian nationalists for undermining fundamental legal principles.

What was the most objectionable aspect of these Acts?

options.text: They imposed heavy taxes on Indian businesses and traders.
They mandated the compulsory registration of all Indian citizens
They allowed the government to detain individuals without trial based on suspicion of revolutionary activities
They granted greater powers to local self-governing bodies.

solution:
The correct answer is __**They allowed the government to detain individuals without trial based on suspicion of revolutionary activities**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e3594069eb4eac3d559af7c626aabe4ee4145967932cf8ad78e35476f134a4b8.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act of 1919**, popularly known as the **Rowlatt Act**, was passed by the **Imperial Legislative Council** in **Delhi** on **March 18, 1919**.
 
• The most contentious provision of this legislation was the authorization of the **British colonial government** to arrest and imprison individuals suspected of **sedition** or **revolutionary activities** for up to **two years** without a jury trial or any judicial proceedings.
 
• This act effectively suspended the principle of **Habeas Corpus**, a legal recourse that protects individuals against arbitrary state detention, thereby granting the executive branch unchecked power over personal liberty.
 
• Indian leaders and nationalists condemned the law as the **Black Act**, describing it with the slogan **No Dalil, No Vakil, No Appeal**, highlighting the denial of the right to legal counsel, the right to present evidence, and the right to appeal.
 
• The act was intended to suppress the growing **nationalist upsurge** and political unrest that followed **World War I** by providing extraordinary powers to the police and administration.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Rowlatt Committee and Aftermath:**

 
 
• The legislation was based on the recommendations of the **Sedition Committee**, headed by **Justice Sidney Rowlatt**, which was tasked with investigating **revolutionary conspiracies** in India.
 
• In protest, **Mahatma Gandhi** organized the **Rowlatt Satyagraha**, calling for a nationwide **Hartal** (strike) on **April 6, 1919**, which marked his first major entry into **Indian national politics**.
 
• The severe government crackdown on these protests directly culminated in the tragic **Jallianwala Bagh Massacre** on **April 13, 1919**, in **Amritsar**.
 
 
 
• **Context of Other Options:**
 
 
• **Compulsory registration** of citizens was a feature of the **Asiatic Registration Act** in the **Transvaal** (South Africa), which Gandhi had previously fought against in **1906**.
 
• The **Rowlatt Act** was specifically designed for **political suppression** rather than **economic taxation** or the empowerment of **local self-governing bodies**.
